The functional contrasts between sentences characterized by right branching vs. center embedding or unambiguous vs. ambiguous relative clause attachment are also picked up by ID, but in a less marked way, and they do not correlate with the same processing phase. Further experiments using representational similarity and layer ablation confirm the same trends. We conclude that ID is a useful marker of linguistic complexity in LLMs, that it allows to differentiate between different types of complexity, and that it points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.

papers.title: Characterizing the Role of Similarity in the Property Inferences of Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models perform property inheritance, and what roles do taxonomic relations and categorical similarities play in this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Language models' property inheritance behavior is jointly explained by taxonomic relations and categorical similarity, and these features are entangled in the model's internal representations.
papers.conclusion: LMs perform property inheritance with sensitivity to both taxonomic relations and similarity, and these two factors are entangled in their internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
LMs show high taxonomic sensitivity in property inheritance, but also positive correlation with similarity between categories.
LMs are more likely to extend a property when categories are taxonomically related and highly similar.
Causal analysis reveals that the subspaces responsible for property inheritance reflect both taxonomic and similarity features.
Taxonomy and similarity are fundamentally entangled in LM representations, even when trained on unambiguous taxonomic data.
LMs exhibit graded property inheritance behavior similar to humans, influenced by similarity.
papers.limitation:
Alternative similarities could have been used, such as WordNet similarities or LM-derived similarities.
The study focuses only on concrete object noun concepts, not abstract or ad-hoc concepts.
The work does not engage with knowledge editing, which could be an interesting extension.
Property inheritance is only one type of inductive problem; broader generalization is not studied.
Similarity in inductive problems can be context-sensitive, which is not accounted for with nonce properties.
future_direction: Exploring other similarity measures and their correlation with property inheritance.
Extending the investigation to abstract and ad-hoc concepts.
Testing the entanglement of taxonomy and similarity in human property inheritance.
papers.abstract: Property inheritance -- a phenomenon where novel properties are projected from higher level categories (e.g., birds) to lower level ones (e.g., sparrows) -- provides a unique window into how humans organize and deploy conceptual knowledge. It is debated whether this ability arises due to explicitly stored taxonomic knowledge vs. simple computations of similarity between mental representations. How are these mechanistic hypotheses manifested in contemporary language models? In this work, we investigate how LMs perform property inheritance with behavioral and causal representational analysis experiments. We find that taxonomy and categorical similarities are not mutually exclusive in LMs' property inheritance behavior. That is, LMs are more likely to project novel properties from one category to the other when they are taxonomically related and at the same time, highly similar. Our findings provide insight into the conceptual structure of language models and may suggest new psycholinguistic experiments for human subjects.

papers.title: Word class representations spontaneously emerge in a deep neural network trained on next word prediction
papers.research_question: Whether abstract linguistic categories, such as word classes, can emerge spontaneously in a neural network trained on next word prediction, without explicit supervision.
papers.core_contribution: Word class representations spontaneously emerge in a deep neural network trained on next word prediction, suggesting such categories can be learned from statistical regularities without innate knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Word classes can emerge from predictive processing during language acquisition, challenging the notion of innate grammatical categories.
papers.key_findings:
Internal representations of nine-word input sequences cluster according to the word class of the tenth word to be predicted.
Clustering becomes stronger in deeper layers of the network, as shown by the decreasing GDV.
The network organizes its internal representations of language input according to abstract linguistic categories without explicit supervision.
papers.abstract: How do humans learn language, and can the first language be learned at all? These fundamental questions are still hotly debated. In contemporary linguistics, there are two major schools of thought that give completely opposite answers. According to Chomsky's theory of universal grammar, language cannot be learned because children are not exposed to sufficient data in their linguistic environment. In contrast, usage-based models of language assume a profound relationship between language structure and language use. In particular, contextual mental processing and mental representations are assumed to have the cognitive capacity to capture the complexity of actual language use at all levels. The prime example is syntax, i.e., the rules by which words are assembled into larger units such as sentences. Typically, syntactic rules are expressed as sequences of word classes. However, it remains unclear whether word classes are innate, as implied by universal grammar, or whether they emerge during language acquisition, as suggested by usage-based approaches. Here, we address this issue from a machine learning and natural language processing perspective. In particular, we trained an artificial deep neural network on predicting the next word, provided sequences of consecutive words as input. Subsequently, we analyzed the emerging activation patterns in the hidden layers of the neural network. Strikingly, we find that the internal representations of nine-word input sequences cluster according to the word class of the tenth word to be predicted as output, even though the neural network did not receive any explicit information about syntactic rules or word classes during training. This surprising result suggests, that also in the human brain, abstract representational categories such as word classes may naturally emerge as a consequence of predictive coding and processing during language acquisition.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: Latent Knowledge as a Predictor of Fact Acquisition in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does latent knowledge in a pretrained model predict the rate of fact acquisition, generalization, and degradation during fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a survival-analysis framework to model fact acquisition as a time-to-event process and shows that latent knowledge is the strongest predictor of fact acquisition rate and generalization during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Latent knowledge acquired during pretraining influences the rate of fact acquisition during fine-tuning and predicts which unseen ontology facts will generalize. By contrast, resistance to degradation depends on whether facts are reinforced during training.
papers.key_findings:
Latent knowledge is the strongest predictor of fact acquisition rate (hazard ratio 2.6).
Facts with latent knowledge are learned earlier, at higher peak rates, and converge sooner.
Generalization to unseen GO terms is uncommon (5.8%) but more likely for terms with latent knowledge.
Degradation of previously correct mappings is more likely for unseen terms than seen terms, indicating a protective effect of training.
Identifier frequency and annotation counts have smaller but significant effects on acquisition rate, while raw term frequency does not.
papers.limitation:
The study operationalizes factual acquisition using term-identifier pairs, and the extent to which this generalizes to other types of biomedical facts warrants further investigation.
The fine-tuning experiments used a fixed hyperparameter configuration and only up to 20 epochs; longer training might yield different results.
The Cox proportional hazards model hazard ratios are not constant over time, so the reported values represent average effects and may mask interactions with training epoch.
The analysis does not examine internal mechanisms (e.g., shifts in logits, parameter updates, or representational geometry) that drive fact acquisition.
The method is computationally intensive, requiring repeated stochastic-decoding queries per term and evaluation of the full test set at each fine-tuning epoch.
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic analyses with the proposed time-to-event framework.
Extending the approach to skill-based domains such as reasoning or multi-step tool use.
Investigating the generalization of the framework to other types of biomedical facts.
papers.abstract: Large language models store biomedical facts with uneven strength after pretraining: some facts are present in the weights but are not reliably accessible under deterministic decoding (latent knowledge), while others are scarcely represented. We fine tuned Llama 3.1 8B Instruct to learn ontology term identifier mappings from the Human Phenotype Ontology (800 pairs) and the Gene Ontology (400 training pairs), withholding 400 GO pairs to test generalization. Treating learning as a time to event process across 20 epochs, we used stochastic decoding to detect latent knowledge at baseline and Cox proportional hazards models to identify predictors of acquisition, generalization, and degradation. Baseline deterministic recall for HPO was 2.8%, rising to 71.9% after fine-tuning. Latent knowledge was the strongest predictor of faster fact acquisition (HR 2.6) and was associated with earlier, higher peak learning rates and faster convergence; identifier frequency and curated annotation counts had smaller effects. Generalization to withheld GO facts was uncommon (5.8%) but more likely when latent knowledge was present. Previously correct GO mappings degraded more often for withheld (unseen) terms than for trained (seen) terms, suggesting a protective effect of reinforcement during training. These results show that latent knowledge predicts both the speed of factual learning during fine-tuning and the limited generalization of unseen ontology facts, while resistance to degradation depends on whether facts are reinforced.

papers.title: Left-right asymmetry in predicting brain activity from LLMs' representations emerges with their formal linguistic competence
papers.research_question: What competence acquired by LLMs during training underlies the emergence of left-right asymmetry in brain predictivity?
papers.core_contribution: The left-right asymmetry in brain predictivity emerges specifically with the acquisition of formal linguistic competence (grammatical knowledge) in LLMs, not with other competencies like arithmetic or functional language understanding.
papers.conclusion: The emergence of left-right asymmetry in brain predictivity is a direct reflection of LLMs' acquisition of formal linguistic abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Left-right asymmetry in brain scores emerges during training of LLMs.
This asymmetry co-occurs with the emergence of formal linguistic abilities (as measured by BLiMP, Zorro, and linguistic acceptability of generated text).
The asymmetry does not correlate with performance on non-linguistic tasks (arithmetic and Dyck language).
The asymmetry does not correlate with performance on functional linguistic tasks involving world knowledge and reasoning (ARC and Hellaswag).
The results generalize to other LLM families (Pythia) and to another language (French).
papers.limitation: Brain scores may not be driven solely by syntactic knowledge; semantic content also plays a role, as indicated by prior work.
future_direction: More work is needed to understand the development of more sophisticated linguistic capabilities and how it translates into the alignment between artificial and biological neural processing.
Future work will address whether similar links between brain regions and LLMs at different training steps exist for language.
papers.abstract: When humans and large language models (LLMs) process the same text, activations in the LLMs correlate with brain activity measured, e.g., with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Moreover, it has been shown that, as the training of an LLM progresses, the performance in predicting brain activity from its internal activations improves more in the left hemisphere than in the right one. The aim of the present work is to understand which kind of competence acquired by the LLMs underlies the emergence of this left-right asymmetry. Using the OLMo-2 7B language model at various training checkpoints and fMRI data from English participants, we compare the evolution of the left-right asymmetry in brain scores alongside performance on several benchmarks. We observe that the asymmetry co-emerges with the formal linguistic abilities of the LLM. These abilities are demonstrated in two ways: by the model's capacity to assign a higher probability to an acceptable sentence than to a grammatically unacceptable one within a minimal contrasting pair, or its ability to produce well-formed text. On the opposite, the left-right asymmetry does not correlate with the performance on arithmetic or Dyck language tasks; nor with text-based tasks involving world knowledge and reasoning. We generalize these results to another family of LLMs (Pythia) and another language, namely French. Our observations indicate that the left-right asymmetry in brain predictivity matches the progress in formal linguistic competence (knowledge of linguistic patterns).

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: "SIMULATION OF DEVELOPMENTAL TRANSITIONS BELOW AND ABOVE FORMAL REASONING IN A NEURAL NETWORK MODEL"
papers.research_question: How can neural networks simulate developmental transitions in reasoning stages, and what can structural changes in the model reveal about these transitions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a neural network simulation method for developmental transitions, showing that segregating inputs by order of hierarchical complexity improves performance and reveals different transition patterns based on structural changes.
papers.conclusion: The methodology allows identifying how networked systems represent developmental transitions at different orders of hierarchical complexity, and the OHC is a valid and reliable measure to capture the complexity of problem solving in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Segregating inputs by disjoint order of hierarchical complexity (OHC) led to the best performance of networks in formal-order subtasks (torque difference calculus).
Developmental transitions are represented by the recruitment of new neurons and connections from one OHC network to the next.
Two types of transitions were found: memory-based transitions below formal stages (no change in neurons, slight increase in connections) and operationally-based transitions at and above formal stages (increase in neurons and connections).
More than one transition pattern was observed, indicating self-organization dynamics, with specific increases in neurons and connections across stages.
The model structure for each complexity problem was searched separately, validating OHC as a measure of problem complexity captured by neural networks.
papers.limitation: Limitations concern the operations that were being learned at each OHC subtask, which conflict with the mathematical nature of neural network models.
future_direction: Explore the memory-based transition in future work in the domain of pre-formal stages.
Simulate more complex configurations, namely quadratic sum, to continue exploring the increase in structural complexity throughout post-formal simulations.
papers.abstract: The Model of Hierarchical Complexity (MHC) is one post-Piagetian theory that shows that humans develop through stages beyond post-formal reasoning. At each developmental transition, simpler knowledge self-organizes into more complex knowledge without overwriting itself, however, the nature of transitions is poorly understood. We used neural networks to simulate this stage incremental process and to explore whether conclusions about transitions could be taken from the developing structure of the model, specifically when solving problems below and above formal reasoning. We simulated stage-wise human performance on the balance-beam test. The MHC analyzed the order of hierarchical complexity (OHC) of balance-beam tasks, identifying 4 OHC subtasks (9, 10, 11, and 12), each being solved by individuals at the following stages: concrete (stage-9), abstract (stage-10), formal (stage11) and systematic (stage-12). Hence, two stages below formal, where individuals operate with concrete information until they transform it into abstract information, and two stages above formal, where individuals operate with abstract information. In our method, we segregated the input set into the four disjoint OHC subsets. Then, we trained the minimal neural network model structure to solve each OHC subset separately. The best performing model for each OHC subset was selected and the evolving structure across sequential models was evaluated. Developmental transitions are represented by the recruitment of new neurons and connections from one OHC network to the next. First, results showed that segregating inputs by disjoint OHC led to the best performance of networks in the formal-order subtasks (torque difference calculus) among the literature. Second, transitions from concrete to abstract rely mostly upon an increase of memory resources of the existing connections. From abstract to formal and from formal to systematic, there is an increase in the number of neurons and connections. More than one transition pattern was found, which points towards the dynamic of self-organization. We either observed that there is an increase of 120% in both the number of neurons and connections from abstract to formal and a decrease of 50% from formal to systematic or that there is an increase of 80% in the number of neurons and connections, which maintains stable during the systematic performance. Limitations of this work concern the operations that were being learned at each OHC subtask, which conflict with the mathematical nature of neural network models. Even so, the scaling of network elements is worth exploring by simulating further OHC subtasks.

papers.title: Evidence from fMRI Supports a Two-Phase Abstraction Process in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are intermediate layers of LLMs, rather than output layers, most predictive of brain activity? Is this due to the abstraction/composition process or the next-token prediction objective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that the similarity between LLM representations and brain activity is driven by the abstraction/composition process within LLMs, not by their next-token prediction objective. This is supported by a strong correlation between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations.
papers.conclusion: The abstraction process in LLMs, characterized by increasing intrinsic dimensionality in intermediate layers, is supported by evidence from fMRI encoding models and is the primary driver of brain-model similarity, rather than the next-token prediction objective.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding performance for predicting brain activity and the intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of layer representations are highly correlated across layers and model sizes.
A two-phase process exists in LLMs: an early abstraction/composition phase (where Id and encoding performance increase) followed by a later prediction phase (where Id decreases and next-token prediction loss drops sharply).
The peak of encoding performance and Id shifts to earlier layers as training progresses, indicating the abstraction phase becomes more compressed.
The relationship between encoding performance and Id emerges during training and is not a trivial function of architecture or layer index.
Brain regions involved in higher-level linguistic processing show a stronger correlation between encoding performance and Id than low-level auditory cortex.
papers.limitation:
The study only tests two model families (OPT and Pythia), so conclusions may not generalize to all LLMs.
It is inherently challenging to draw affirmative conclusions about underlying brain mechanisms from brain-model similarity alone.
future_direction: Test the findings on more model families to establish generalizability.
Explore methods to combine representations from different layers to create a representation with higher intrinsic dimensionality and potentially better encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models are able to predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most capable for this unique and highly general transfer task? In this work, we show that evidence from language encoding models in fMRI supports the existence of a two-phase abstraction process within LLMs. We use manifold learning methods to show that this abstraction process naturally arises over the course of training a language model and that the first "composition" phase of this abstraction process is compressed into fewer layers as training continues. Finally, we demonstrate a strong correspondence between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations from LLMs. We give initial evidence that this correspondence primarily derives from the inherent compositionality of LLMs and not their next-word prediction properties.

papers.title: Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-modal large language models lack core knowledge, i.e., rudimentary cognitive abilities that are innate in humans from early childhood?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the CoreCognition benchmark for evaluating core knowledge in MLLMs and finds that MLLMs exhibit significant deficits in low-level core abilities, show misaligned dependencies between abilities, and rely on shortcut learning rather than genuine understanding as they scale.
papers.conclusion: MLLMs exhibit significant deficits in core knowledge, and scaling does not lead to genuine understanding but instead increases reliance on shortcut learning.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs consistently perform worse on low-level core abilities compared to high-level abilities.
MLLM performance on high-level abilities is not correlated with the underlying low-level abilities that support them.
MLLMs exhibit less, or even no, scalability on low-level abilities compared to high-level abilities as model parameters increase.
Models increasing in size exhibit core deficits and shortcut-taking behaviors rather than progressing toward conceptual understanding.
The proposed Concept Hacking method reveals MLLMs fail to achieve genuine core knowledge understanding and instead rely on shortcut learning.
papers.abstract: While Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate impressive abilities over high-level perception and reasoning, their robustness in the wild remains limited, often falling short on tasks that are intuitive and effortless for humans. We examine the hypothesis that these deficiencies stem from the absence of core knowledge--rudimentary cognitive abilities innate to humans from early childhood. To explore the core knowledge representation in MLLMs, we introduce CoreCognition, a large-scale benchmark encompassing 12 core knowledge concepts grounded in developmental cognitive science. We evaluate 230 models with 11 different prompts, leading to a total of 2,530 data points for analysis. Our experiments uncover four key findings, collectively demonstrating core knowledge deficits in MLLMs: they consistently underperform and show reduced, or even absent, scalability on low-level abilities relative to high-level ones. Finally, we propose Concept Hacking, a novel controlled evaluation method that reveals MLLMs fail to progress toward genuine core knowledge understanding, but instead rely on shortcut learning as they scale.

papers.title: Discovering Latent Concepts Learned in BERT
papers.research_question: What latent concepts exist in the pre-trained BERT model, how do the discovered latent concepts align or diverge from classical linguistic hierarchy, and how do the latent concepts evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised method to discover and analyze latent concepts learned in BERT, and releases a novel multi-facet hierarchical concept dataset (BCN).
papers.conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive analysis of latent concepts in BERT and releases a novel BERT-centric concept dataset (BCN) that facilitates future interpretation studies and serves as an annotated resource.
papers.key_findings:
BERT learns novel concepts (e.g., animal categories, demographic groups) that do not strictly adhere to pre-defined linguistic categories.
Many latent concepts are based on multiple properties (e.g., semantics, syntax, morphology).
Lower layers dominate in learning shallow lexical concepts, while higher layers learn semantic relations.
The discovered latent concepts highlight potential biases learned in the model (e.g., gender and demographic associations).
Concepts learned at higher layers are more aligned with linguistically motivated concepts compared to lower layers.
papers.limitation:
The diversity of observed concepts is limited by the dataset and clustering constraints (memory and algorithm).
Only the final layer of BERT was manually annotated due to annotation cost.
The method is limited to word-level concepts; phrase-level concepts are not explored.
future_direction: Increase diversity of concepts by working around memory and algorithm constraints.
Explore phrase-level concepts.
Incorporate principal component analysis for more controlled analysis.
papers.abstract: A large number of studies that analyze deep neural network models and their ability to encode various linguistic and non-linguistic concepts provide an interpretation of the inner mechanics of these models. The scope of the analyses is limited to pre-defined concepts that reinforce the traditional linguistic knowledge and do not reflect on how novel concepts are learned by the model. We address this limitation by discovering and analyzing latent concepts learned in neural network models in an unsupervised fashion and provide interpretations from the model's perspective. In this work, we study: i) what latent concepts exist in the pre-trained BERT model, ii) how the discovered latent concepts align or diverge from classical linguistic hierarchy and iii) how the latent concepts evolve across layers. Our findings show: i) a model learns novel concepts (e.g. animal categories and demographic groups), which do not strictly adhere to any pre-defined categorization (e.g. POS, semantic tags), ii) several latent concepts are based on multiple properties which may include semantics, syntax, and morphology, iii) the lower layers in the model dominate in learning shallow lexical concepts while the higher layers learn semantic relations and iv) the discovered latent concepts highlight potential biases learned in the model. We also release a novel BERT ConceptNet dataset (BCN) consisting of 174 concept labels and 1M annotated instances.

papers.title: Abstraction in time: Finding hierarchical linguistic structure in a model of relational processing
papers.research_question: Does the oscillatory activation in LISA/DORA models during processing match human cortical activity during language processing, suggesting a common mechanism for hierarchical representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LISA/DORA models of relational processing exhibit oscillatory activation patterns during sentence processing that closely match human cortical tracking of hierarchical linguistic structures, suggesting that mechanisms for relational binding may underlie language representation.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that abstract hierarchical linguistic representations can be processed by models of relational reasoning, and suggests that integrating such models with language processing models could advance cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
LISA/DORA models parse English sentences and show firing patterns that mirror cortical activity observed in Ding et al. (2016), with activation bursts at sentence (1Hz), phrasal (2Hz), and syllabic (4Hz) rates.
The models' binding mechanisms, using temporal synchrony and asynchrony, naturally produce hierarchical representations similar to those in human language processing.
These models, built for analogy and relational learning, generalize to language processing without modification, unlike grammar-based or statistical models.
The results support the idea that relational role representation may be a foundation for human cognitive capacities like language.
Integrating models of relational reasoning and language processing could lead to more plausible cognitive models.
future_direction: Testing on natural speech input
Testing on varied syntactic structures
Testing in rich discourse contexts and multilingual input
papers.abstract: Abstract mental representation is fundamental for human cognition. Forming such representations in time, especially from dynamic and noisy perceptual input, is a challenge for any processing modality, but perhaps none so acutely as for language processing. We show that LISA (Hummel & Holyaok, 1997) and DORA (Doumas, Hummel, & Sandhofer, 2008), models built to process and to learn structured (i.e., symbolic) rep resentations of conceptual properties and relations from unstructured inputs, show oscillatory activation during processing that is highly similar to the cortical activity elicited by the linguistic stimuli from Ding et al.(2016). We argue, as Ding et al.(2016), that this activation reflects formation of hierarchical linguistic representation, and furthermore, that the kind of computational mechanisms in LISA/DORA (e.g., temporal binding by systematic asynchrony of firing) may underlie formation of abstract linguistic representations in the human brain. It may be this repurposing that allowed for the generation or mergence of hierarchical linguistic structure, and therefore, human language, from extant cognitive and neural systems. We conclude that models of thinking and reasoning and models of language processing must be integrated —not only for increased plausiblity, but in order to advance both fields towards a larger integrative model of human cognition

papers.title: Visual Grounding Helps Learn Word Meanings in Low-Data Regimes
papers.research_question: Do models trained with visual grounding exhibit more human-like language learning, specifically in word learning, and are they more efficient in low-data regimes?
papers.core_contribution: Visual supervision improves word learning efficiency in low-data regimes, but benefits are limited and often canceled out when combined with distributional text signals; current models fail to effectively integrate visual and textual information.
papers.conclusion: Visual grounding helps neural models acquire some word knowledge more efficiently than text alone in low-data regimes, but ungrounded models become comparable or better with large data, and current algorithms fail to integrate visual and distributional information effectively.
papers.key_findings:
Visual + Word models learn word similarity and semantic features more efficiently than Language-Only models in low-data regimes.
Visual + Word models perform worse on lexical relation prediction and part-of-speech prediction.
Visual and distributional information compete; current learning algorithms struggle to integrate them.
Visual input helps learn concrete words more than abstract words.
Visual information is unhelpful for sentence processing benchmarks (context-based word understanding and brain-response prediction).
papers.limitation:
Visual information only contains static images, not dynamic visual streams or other modalities available to human learners.
Only three multi-modality learning algorithms (CLIP, GIT, Flamingo) are evaluated.
future_direction: Develop grounded LMs that better integrate visual and distributional information.
Evaluate on visual inputs more similar to those received by children (e.g., dynamic streams).
Test more multi-modality learning algorithms.
papers.abstract: Modern neural language models (LMs) are powerful tools for modeling human sentence production and comprehension, and their internal representations are remarkably well-aligned with representations of language in the human brain. But to achieve these results, LMs must be trained in distinctly un-human-like ways - requiring orders of magnitude more language data than children receive during development, and without perceptual or social context. Do models trained more naturalistically -- with grounded supervision -- exhibit more humanlike language learning? We investigate this question in the context of word learning, a key sub-task in language acquisition. We train a diverse set of LM architectures, with and without auxiliary visual supervision, on datasets of varying scales. We then evaluate these models' learning of syntactic categories, lexical relations, semantic features, word similarity, and alignment with human neural representations. We find that visual supervision can indeed improve the efficiency of word learning. However, these improvements are limited: they are present almost exclusively in the low-data regime, and sometimes canceled out by the inclusion of rich distributional signals from text. The information conveyed by text and images is not redundant -- models mainly driven by visual information yield qualitatively different from those mainly driven by word co-occurrences. However, our results suggest that current multimodal modeling approaches fail to effectively leverage visual information to build human-like word representations from human-scale data.

papers.title: Language Models Learn POS First
papers.research_question: How and when are linguistic structures, such as part-of-speech tagging and global topic information, acquired during the training of language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that during training, language models acquire part-of-speech tagging early and global topic information continuously, using methods like gradient concentration and SVCCA.
papers.conclusion: Early training focuses on learning part-of-speech syntax for initial performance, while later training shifts to refining global topic representations for further gains.
papers.key_findings:
Frequent words have more concentrated gradients, and concentration increases over time during training.
Closed POS classes (e.g., pronouns, prepositions) show early concentration stabilization, while open classes (e.g., nouns, verbs) continue to become more concentrated.
Part-of-speech tagging is learned early in training, with representation peaking before the first optimizer step size rescale.
Global topic information is learned continuously throughout training, with representation increasing over time.
future_direction: Develop ways of interpreting syntactic structures during training.
papers.abstract: A glut of recent research shows that language models capture linguistic structure. Such work answers the question of whether a model represents linguistic structure. But how and when are these structures acquired? Rather than treating the training process itself as a black box, we investigate how representations of linguistic structure are learned over time. In particular, we demonstrate that different aspects of linguistic structure are learned at different rates, with part of speech tagging acquired early and global topic information learned continuously.

papers.title: Vision-Language Models Align with Human Neural Representations in Concept Processing
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models (VLMs) from different families align with human neural representations in concept processing, and how does visual or textual context affect this alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Vision-language models (VLMs) align with human neural representations in concept processing, with vision-language encoders showing higher alignment than generative VLMs, and for some VLMs the alignment stems from learning human-like concepts during pretraining rather than just context at inference.
papers.conclusion: VLMs, particularly vision-language encoders, align with human neural representations in concept processing, and their advantage stems from learning multimodal semantic information during pretraining, not just from context at inference.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs outperform language-only models in aligning with human brain responses in both sentence and picture conditions.
Vision-language encoders (VisualBERT, LXMERT) are more brain-aligned than contrastive and generative VLMs.
In the sentence condition, only VisualBERT and LXMERT significantly outperform BERT, while generative VLMs do not outperform their language-only counterparts.
Ablation studies show that for LXMERT and IDEFICS2, brain alignment is less sensitive to input images, indicating learning of human-like concepts during pretraining.
Generative VLMs show lower brain alignment compared to vision-language encoders, despite their superior performance on downstream tasks.
papers.limitation:
VLMs differ along many dimensions (size, architecture, learning objective, training data), making it hard to attribute differences in brain alignment to one specific factor.
The brain regions of interest (ROIs) considered may not capture all regions involved in multimodal integration.
Averaging brain responses across participants may smooth out participant-specific patterns.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that transformer-based vision-language models (VLMs) capture the multimodality of concept processing in the human brain. However, a systematic evaluation exploring different types of VLM architectures and the role played by visual and textual context is still lacking. Here, we analyse multiple VLMs employing different strategies to integrate visual and textual modalities, along with language-only counterparts. We measure the alignment between concept representations by models and existing (fMRI) brain responses to concept words presented in two experimental conditions, where either visual (pictures) or textual (sentences) context is provided. Our results reveal that VLMs outperform the language-only counterparts in both experimental conditions. However, controlled ablation studies show that only for some VLMs, such as LXMERT and IDEFICS2, brain alignment stems from genuinely learning more human-like concepts during pretraining, while others are highly sensitive to the context provided at inference. Additionally, we find that vision-language encoders are more brain-aligned than more recent, generative VLMs. Altogether, our study shows that VLMs align with human neural representations in concept processing, while highlighting differences among architectures. We open-source code and materials to reproduce our experiments at: https://github.com/dmg-illc/vl-concept-processing.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Model Organisms for Human Associative Learning
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit representational dynamics akin to human associative learning, and can they help disambiguate between competing hypotheses for representational change? How does vocabulary interference modulate representational change?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit a non-monotonic pattern of representational change during associative learning (consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis), and this change is modulated by vocabulary interference, with higher interference leading to stronger differentiation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can serve as accessible and general computational models for studying human associative learning, providing new insights into how local pair similarity and global competition shape representational change.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show three distinct phases of learning during in-context associative learning: encoding (accuracy increases), consolidation (accuracy stabilizes), and forgetting (accuracy declines).
During the consolidation phase, moderately similar token pairs significantly differentiate, producing a U-shaped pattern of representational change that aligns with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis.
Vocabulary interference—the similarity between a paired item and the model's prior knowledge—modulates representational change: higher interference leads to stronger differentiation.
The non-monotonic differentiation pattern is only present during consolidation and disappears during encoding and forgetting phases.
These representational dynamics are consistent across six different open-source LLMs, despite architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
The token pairs used are synthetic and optimized for similarity, which may not reflect naturalistic learning scenarios.
The forgetting phase is not well understood, and its causes require further investigation.
LLMs are not biologically plausible models of the brain, limiting direct comparisons to neural mechanisms.
future_direction: Investigating the causes of forgetting and predicting when it occurs.
Extending the analysis to more naturalistic stimuli and real-world associative learning tasks.
Exploring how different model architectures (e.g., with explicit memory modules) affect representational dynamics.
papers.abstract: Associative learning--forming links between co-occurring items--is fundamental to human cognition, reshaping internal representations in complex ways. Testing hypotheses on how representational changes occur in biological systems is challenging, but large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative. Building on LLMs' in-context learning, we adapt a cognitive neuroscience associative learning paradigm and investigate how representations evolve across six models. Our initial findings reveal a non-monotonic pattern consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis, with moderately similar items differentiating after learning. Leveraging the controllability of LLMs, we further show that this differentiation is modulated by the overlap of associated items with the broader vocabulary--a factor we term vocabulary interference, capturing how new associations compete with prior knowledge. We find that higher vocabulary interference amplifies differentiation, suggesting that representational change is influenced by both item similarity and global competition. Our findings position LLMs not only as powerful tools for studying representational dynamics in human-like learning systems, but also as accessible and general computational models for generating new hypotheses about the principles underlying memory reorganization in the brain.

papers.title: Insights on Neural Representations for End-to-End Speech Recognition
papers.research_question: How do neural representations correlate across layers and training in end-to-end ASR models, and how does this relate to model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides insights into hierarchical correlation dependencies in CNN layers, bottom-up patterns in LSTM, and irregular correlations in Transformer layers for end-to-end ASR, showing how CCA and CKA can analyze neural representations and identify pathological components.
papers.conclusion: A comparative analysis of SVCCA and CKA identified pathological components in CNN and Transformer models, and these techniques can be used to gain insights into neural representations for building better ASR models.
papers.key_findings:
CNN layers exhibit hierarchical correlation dependencies as layer depth increases.
LSTM architecture shows a bottom-up pattern across the training process.
Transformer encoder layers exhibit irregular correlation as neural depth increases.
SVCCA is more sensitive to initialization parameters and under-represents neural representations compared to CKA.
CKA can visualize pathology in neural representations during training, especially in Transformer models.
papers.limitation:
SVCCA's SVD component relies on the reflection of class information, which is a potential limitation for end-to-end speech recognition.
CKA has high computational costs for large models due to size and computational requirements.
future_direction: Compare correlation of trained neural layers across different speech datasets, such as noisy or augmented data.
Analyze neural representations on out-of-domain data.
Explore few-shot-learning in ASR using these insights.
papers.abstract:
End-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) models aim to learn a
generalised speech representation. However, there are limited tools available
to understand the internal functions and the effect of hierarchical
dependencies within the model architecture. It is crucial to understand the
correlations between the layer-wise representations, to derive insights on the
relationship between neural representations and performance.
 Previous investigations of network similarities using correlation analysis
techniques have not been explored for End-to-End ASR models. This paper
analyses and explores the internal dynamics between layers during training with
CNN, LSTM and Transformer based approaches using Canonical correlation analysis
(CCA) and centered kernel alignment (CKA) for the experiments. It was found
that neural representations within CNN layers exhibit hierarchical correlation
dependencies as layer depth increases but this is mostly limited to cases where
neural representation correlates more closely. This behaviour is not observed
in LSTM architecture, however there is a bottom-up pattern observed across the
training process, while Transformer encoder layers exhibit irregular
coefficiency correlation as neural depth increases. Altogether, these results
provide new insights into the role that neural architectures have upon speech
recognition performance. More specifically, these techniques can be used as
indicators to build better performing speech recognition models.

papers.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
papers.research_question: Can editing representations, instead of weights, be a more powerful alternative for parameter-efficient finetuning of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representation Finetuning (ReFT), a family of parameter-efficient finetuning methods that edit hidden representations instead of weights, and shows that it is more parameter-efficient and often outperforms existing PEFTs.
papers.conclusion: ReFT methods are a promising alternative to weight-based PEFTs, offering a better balance of efficiency and performance, and are worthy of further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
ReFT methods are 15×–65× more parameter-efficient than LoRA.
LoReFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on commonsense reasoning, instruction-following, and natural language understanding.
ReFT methods are less effective on arithmetic reasoning tasks, possibly due to the length of chain-of-thought generations.
ReFT performance scales with model size.
LoReFT outperforms full finetuning on instruction-following with only 0.0039% of parameters.
papers.limitation: ReFTs may have trouble with chain-of-thought reasoning tasks due to the length of generations and overall greater difficulty of the task.
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods seek to adapt large neural models via updates to a small number of weights. However, much prior interpretability work has shown that representations encode rich semantic information, suggesting that editing representations might be a more powerful alternative. We pursue this hypothesis by developing a family of Representation Finetuning (ReFT) methods. ReFT methods operate on a frozen base model and learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations. We define a strong instance of the ReFT family, Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT), and we identify an ablation of this method that trades some performance for increased efficiency. Both are drop-in replacements for existing PEFTs and learn interventions that are 15x--65x more parameter-efficient than LoRA. We showcase LoReFT on eight commonsense reasoning tasks, four arithmetic reasoning tasks, instruction-tuning, and GLUE. In all these evaluations, our ReFTs deliver the best balance of efficiency and performance, and almost always outperform state-of-the-art PEFTs. We release a generic ReFT training library publicly at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: LLMs model how humans induce logically structured rules
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) model human induction of logically structured rules? Do they provide a good fit to human behavior and do they use similar logical or logic-like operators?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can model human logical rule induction as well as Bayesian probabilistic Language of Thought (pLoT) models, and they may instantiate a novel theoretical account of human logical concepts without built-in logical primitives.
papers.conclusion: LLMs provide a good model of human logical rule induction and may offer a new theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations underlying human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.
papers.key_findings:
Some LLMs (e.g., GPT4, Gemma-7b) achieve human-level accuracy on logical rule induction tasks.
When prompted to explain rules, LLMs sometimes produce rules that use logical operators similar to humans.
Tuning an LLM (Gemma-7b) on human responses yields a better fit to human learning trajectories than tuning on correct answers or than Bayesian pLoT models.
The tuned LLM's high correlation with human data is not just due to learning the rules correctly; it captures human-like learning patterns.
The tuning generalizes to held-out rules and to new rule types (e.g., minority/majority judgments).
papers.limitation:
It is hard to know what the LLM learns when tuning to human responses, and it is hard to fully eliminate the concern that the tuning process is introducing an artifact that increases fit even on withheld exemplars.
The held-out rules share components with seen rules, so generalization might not be fully compositional.
future_direction: Investigate the representations and processes LLMs use for logical rule induction.
Compare LLM-based accounts to human cognitive processes more deeply.
papers.abstract: A central goal of cognitive science is to provide a computationally explicit account of both the structure of the mind and its development: what are the primitive representational building blocks of cognition, what are the rules via which those primitives combine, and where do these primitives and rules come from in the first place? A long-standing debate concerns the adequacy of artificial neural networks as computational models that can answer these questions, in particular in domains related to abstract cognitive function, such as language and logic. This paper argues that recent advances in neural networks -- specifically, the advent of large language models (LLMs) -- represent an important shift in this debate. We test a variety of LLMs on an existing experimental paradigm used for studying the induction of rules formulated over logical concepts. Across four experiments, we find converging empirical evidence that LLMs provide at least as good a fit to human behavior as models that implement a Bayesian probablistic language of thought (pLoT), which have been the best computational models of human behavior on the same task. Moreover, we show that the LLMs make qualitatively different predictions about the nature of the rules that are inferred and deployed in order to complete the task, indicating that the LLM is unlikely to be a mere implementation of the pLoT solution. Based on these results, we argue that LLMs may instantiate a novel theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations necessary to explain human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Investigating word learning processes in an artificial agent
papers.research_question: How can we analyze the internal representations of a computational word-learning model to assess its cognitive plausibility and relate it to infant word learning?
papers.core_contribution: Develops novel quantitative methods to analyze internal representations of a computational word-learning model and discusses their ecological validity for child language acquisition.
papers.conclusion: It is difficult to examine computational models in detail and relate them to infant learning, emphasizing the need for tools to inspect internal workings.
papers.key_findings:
The model quickly forms one-to-one associations between keywords and acoustic patterns, and these associations stabilize early.
The model's internal representations continue to evolve even after accuracy plateaus, with updates occurring upon encountering new instances of keywords.
Speaker changes induce stronger updates in keyword columns compared to same-speaker repetitions, indicating sensitivity to speaker characteristics.
Non-keyword columns are necessary for accurate recognition but do not encode interpretable high-level linguistic features.
The model does not develop speaker-dependent representations, likely due to the orthogonal coding of conceptual information.
papers.limitation:
The orthogonal pseudo-visual coding strongly biases the model's internal organization, making more sophisticated representations unlikely to emerge.
The strong binding of acoustic and conceptual information early in training may stem from the orthogonality of the encoding rather than a general learning principle.
future_direction: Further investigation into the impact of conceptual coding schemes on model behavior.
Development of tools to enable detailed inspection of computational models.
papers.abstract: Researchers in human language processing and acquisition are making an increasing use of computational models. Computer simulations provide a valuable platform to reproduce hypothesised learning mechanisms that are otherwise very difficult, if not impossible, to verify on human subjects. However, computational models come with problems and risks. It is difficult to (automatically) extract essential information about the developing internal representations from a set of simulation runs, and often researchers limit themselves to analysing learning curves based on empirical recognition accuracy through time. The associated risk is to erroneously deem a specific learning behaviour as generalisable to human learners, while it could also be a mere consequence (artifact) of the implementation of the artificial learner or of the input coding scheme. In this paper a set of simulation runs taken from the ACORNS project is investigated. First a look `inside the box' of the learner is provided by employing novel quantitative methods for analysing changing structures in large data sets. Then, the obtained findings are discussed in the perspective of their ecological validity in the field of child language acquisition.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how LLMs develop causally functional representations of semantic roles, specifically focusing on the localization, emergence dynamics, and cross-scale/cross-family generalization of semantic-role circuits.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a causal-temporal method for discovering and tracking semantic-role circuits in LLMs, and finds that these circuits are highly localized, emerge via gradual refinement, and show partial transfer across scales and architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure that exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures, suggesting that transformers encode predicate-argument binding via compact circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic-role information is encoded in compact, role-specific circuits (89–92% attribution within ≤20 nodes).
These circuits emerge via continuous refinement rather than discrete phase transitions.
There is a structure-function dissociation: circuits stabilize structurally before becoming functionally indispensable.
Cross-scale and cross-family analysis shows moderate component reuse (24–51% node overlap) but divergent wiring.
Larger models reuse similar components while rewiring connections.
papers.abstract: Despite displaying semantic competence, large language models' internal mechanisms that ground abstract semantic structure remain insufficiently characterised. We propose a method integrating role-cross minimal pairs, temporal emergence analysis, and cross-model comparison to study how LLMs implement semantic roles. Our analysis uncovers: (i) highly concentrated circuits (89-94% attribution within 28 nodes); (ii) gradual structural refinement rather than phase transitions, with larger models sometimes bypassing localised circuits; and (iii) moderate cross-scale conservation (24-59% component overlap) alongside high spectral similarity. These findings suggest that LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure, and these mechanisms exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do features in language models emerge and evolve internally during pre-training? What is the internal dynamics of model pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using cross-snapshot crosscoders to track the evolution of interpretable features during language model pre-training, revealing a two-phase learning process (statistical then feature learning) and establishing causal connections between feature formation and downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that cross-snapshot crosscoders can successfully track fine-grained feature evolution during pre-training, providing empirical evidence for a statistical-to-feature-learning phase transition and opening possibilities for detailed analysis of representation learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Feature evolution follows a two-phase pattern: a statistical learning phase followed by a feature learning phase, with most features beginning to form around step 1000.
Decoder norms of crosscoder features serve as effective proxies for tracking feature strength and presence across training snapshots.
More complex features (e.g., induction, context-sensitive) tend to emerge later in training than simpler features (e.g., previous token).
Attribution-based circuit tracing shows that the formation of specific crosscoder features causally contributes to improvements on downstream tasks like subject-verb agreement.
Features undergo a universal directional shift around step 1000, after which they rotate more gradually while maintaining similarity to their post-step 1000 orientations.
papers.limitation: Crosscoders may theoretically misalign unrelated features or split shared features across snapshots, though the authors argue these are rare in practice.
papers.abstract: Language models obtain extensive capabilities through pre-training. However, the pre-training process remains a black box. In this work, we track linear interpretable feature evolution across pre-training snapshots using a sparse dictionary learning method called crosscoders. We find that most features begin to form around a specific point, while more complex patterns emerge in later training stages. Feature attribution analyses reveal causal connections between feature evolution and downstream performance. Our feature-level observations are highly consistent with previous findings on Transformer's two-stage learning process, which we term a statistical learning phase and a feature learning phase. Our work opens up the possibility to track fine-grained representation progress during language model learning dynamics.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
