The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: From Words to Waves: Analyzing Concept Formation in Speech and Text-Based Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do conceptual structures in speech models differ from those in text and multimodal models, and to what extent do different modalities yield shared or modality-specific semantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper compares conceptual structures in speech, text, and multimodal models, finding that text models directly encode linguistic taxonomies from early layers, while speech models gradually develop linguistic representations from acoustic features, and multimodal models exhibit unique alignment due to cross-modal training.
papers.conclusion: Text models directly encode linguistic structures from early layers, speech models gradually develop linguistic representations from acoustic features, and multimodal models show unique alignment patterns due to cross-modal training.
papers.key_findings:
Text models directly encode linguistic taxonomies from early layers, while speech models gradually transition from acoustic to linguistic representations.
Multimodal models like SpeechT5 exhibit unique alignment patterns due to cross-modal training.
Speech models allocate less capacity to linguistic and semantic taxonomies, focusing more on speech-specific features like phonetics.
Speech models show weaker performance in capturing negative sentiment compared to text models in task-specific tests.
papers.limitation:
Speech models struggle with tasks requiring deep linguistic reasoning compared to text-based models.
Speech-based sentiment classifiers have difficulty capturing negative sentiment effectively.
future_direction: Integrating additional linguistic or prosodic cues in speech-based models.
Leveraging multi-modal learning strategies.
Exploring alternative architectures to better capture nuances of spoken sentiment.
papers.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated that systems trained solely on text can acquire extensive world knowledge, develop reasoning capabilities, and internalize abstract semantic concepts--showcasing properties that can be associated with general intelligence. This raises an intriguing question: Do such concepts emerge in models trained on other modalities, such as speech? Furthermore, when models are trained jointly on multiple modalities: Do they develop a richer, more structured semantic understanding? To explore this, we analyze the conceptual structures learned by speech and textual models both individually and jointly. We employ Latent Concept Analysis, an unsupervised method for uncovering and interpreting latent representations in neural networks, to examine how semantic abstractions form across modalities. For reproducibility we made scripts and other resources available to the community.

papers.title: A Review of Developmental Interpretability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is developmental interpretability, and how does it help understand the formation and evolution of capabilities in Large Language Models during training?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes the field of developmental interpretability for LLMs, highlighting how understanding training dynamics can provide insights into capability formation and enhance AI safety.
papers.conclusion: Developmental interpretability reveals LLMs as dynamic systems with rich ontogeny, providing a proactive approach to AI safety by understanding capability formation during training.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form through composition of attention heads, enabling in-context learning.
Knowledge acquisition follows a biphasic pattern from formation to optimization.
Emergent abilities arise as phase transitions when pre-training loss crosses critical thresholds.
In-context learning can be transient and replaced by in-weights learning during overtraining.
Grokking involves delayed generalization after memorization.
papers.limitation:
Coverage limitations remain significant across current methodologies.
Feature ontology challenges include poorly defined concepts of what constitutes a 'feature'.
future_direction: Developing a unified theory of developmental dynamics
Creating robust benchmarks and metrics for interpretability
Expanding interpretability to multimodal and agentic AI systems
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the nascent but critical field of developmental interpretability for Large Language Models. We chart the field's evolution from static, post-hoc analysis of trained models to a dynamic investigation of the training process itself. We begin by surveying the foundational methodologies, including representational probing, causal tracing, and circuit analysis, that enable researchers to deconstruct the learning process. The core of this review examines the developmental arc of LLM capabilities, detailing key findings on the formation and composition of computational circuits, the biphasic nature of knowledge acquisition, the transient dynamics of learning strategies like in-context learning, and the phenomenon of emergent abilities as phase transitions in training. We explore illuminating parallels with human cognitive and linguistic development, which provide valuable conceptual frameworks for understanding LLM learning. Finally, we argue that this developmental perspective is not merely an academic exercise but a cornerstone of proactive AI safety, offering a pathway to predict, monitor, and align the processes by which models acquire their capabilities. We conclude by outlining the grand challenges facing the field, such as scalability and automation, and propose a research agenda for building more transparent, reliable, and beneficial AI systems.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: Fresh in memory: Training-order recency is linearly encoded in language model activations
papers.research_question: Do language models linearly encode when information was learned during training? Specifically, is training-order recency encoded in model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Language models linearly encode training-order recency in their activations, and this encoding is robust, generalizable, and accessible to the model itself.
papers.conclusion: Models linearly encode training-order information in their activations, a finding with significant implications for how models might manage conflicting data and respond to knowledge modifications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation centroids for test data from six sequential fine-tuning stages lie on a straight line in a 2D subspace, ordered exactly by training recency.
Linear probes can distinguish entities from the earliest and latest training stages with >90% accuracy, generalizing to held-out entities.
The encoding tracks recency: re-exposing a dataset moves its centroid to the 'most recent' position, and additional training on a stage pushes its centroid further.
The model can be fine-tuned to explicitly report an unseen entity's training stage with ~80% accuracy.
The encoding is not explained by simple activation statistics (norms, moments), output confidence, or geometric properties like PCA directions.
papers.limitation:
The persistence of the training-order signal through mixed-data training complicates a straightforward interpretation that the axis solely tracks exposure recency.
The signal for individual training datapoints (as opposed to entities) is weaker (~60% accuracy) and vanishes after mixed training, suggesting a different mechanism.
future_direction: Exploring whether fine-tuning access can be used to extract information about the order of pretraining data.
Finding a more precise interpretation of the training-order signal that accounts for its persistence through mixed-data training.
papers.abstract: We show that language models' activations linearly encode when information was learned during training. Our setup involves creating a model with a known training order by sequentially fine-tuning Llama-3.2-1B on six disjoint but otherwise similar datasets about named entities. We find that the average activations of test samples corresponding to the six training datasets encode the training order: when projected into a 2D subspace, these centroids are arranged exactly in the order of training and lie on a straight line. Further, we show that linear probes can accurately (~90%) distinguish "early" vs. "late" entities, generalizing to entities unseen during the probes' own training. The model can also be fine-tuned to explicitly report an unseen entity's training stage (~80% accuracy). Interestingly, the training-order encoding does not seem attributable to simple differences in activation magnitudes, losses, or model confidence. Our paper demonstrates that models are capable of differentiating information by its acquisition time, and carries significant implications for how they might manage conflicting data and respond to knowledge modifications.

papers.title: A Self-Organizing Computational Neural Network Architecture with Applications to Sensorimotor Grounded Linguistic Grammar Acquisition
papers.research_question: How can a self-organizing neural network architecture acquire linguistic grammar and demonstrate systematicity, particularly in sensorimotor grounded language acquisition?
papers.core_contribution: This paper develops a novel unsupervised neural network architecture called Chimaera that can acquire separate representations for conceptual and grammatical information, enabling systematic language acquisition and semantic bootstrapping with sensorimotor grounded input.
papers.conclusion: The Chimaera network is capable of acquiring linguistic grammar and demonstrating systematicity, supporting the semantic bootstrapping hypothesis of language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
The Chimaera network can simultaneously store explicit representations of conceptual and grammatical information through a hybrid of self-organizing maps and Hebbian associative networks.
With recurrent processing, the Chimaera network can handle ambiguous grammars and deep n-back transitions efficiently.
Using a co-occurrence-based activation function with sensorimotor grounded input, the network performs semantic bootstrapping to acquire part-of-speech categories.
The network demonstrates systematic behavior on a benchmark grammar test and extends knowledge to novel sensorimotor-grounded words.
It outperforms previous supervised and unsupervised models like Frank (2006) and Farkas & Crocker (2008) in acquiring systematicity.
papers.limitation:
Representing data vectors can be challenging for the network, affecting input representation.
Topography can affect activation and learning dynamics in the self-organizing map.
In feed-forward mode, the network requires many layers to resolve deeply ambiguous grammars, which is computationally inefficient.
future_direction: Extending the network to operate at the lexical level rather than only grammatical category level.
Applying the architecture to other models and domains beyond language acquisition.
Investigating the plausibility of the semantic co-occurrence metric in biological systems.
papers.abstract: Connectionist models of language acquisition typically have difficulty with systematicity, or the ability for the network to generalize its limited experience with language to novel utterances. In this way, connectionist systems learning grammar from a set of example sentences tend to store a set of specific instances, rather than a generalized abstract knowledge of the process of grammatical combination. Further, recent models that do show limited systematicity do so at the expense of simultaneously storing explicit lexical knowledge, and also make use of both developmentally-implausible training data and biologically-implausible learning rules. Consequently, this research program develops a novel unsupervised neural network architecture, and applies this architecture to the problem of systematicity in language models. In the first of several studies, a connectionist architecture capable of simultaneously storing explicit and separate representations of both conceptual and grammatical information is developed, where this architecture is a hybrid of both a self-organizing map and an intra-layer Hebbian associative network. Over the course of several studies, this architecture's capacity to acquire linguistic grammar is evaluated, where the architecture is progressively refined until it is capable of acquiring a benchmark grammar consisting of several difficult clausal sentence structures - though it must acquire this grammar at the level of grammatical category, rather than the lexical level. The final study bridges the gap between the lexical and grammatical category levels, and develops an activation function based on a semantic feature co-occurrence metric. In concert with developmentally-plausible sensorimotor grounded conceptual representations, it is shown that a network using this metric is able to undertake a process of semantic bootstrapping, and successfully acquire separate explicit representations at the level of the concept, part-of-speech category, and grammatical sequence. This network demonstrates broadly systematic behaviour on a difficult test of systematicity, and extends its knowledge of grammar to novel sensorimotor-grounded words.

papers.title: Human-like object concept representations emerge naturally in multimodal large language models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs and MLLMs develop human-like object concept representations through exposure to vast amounts of linguistic and multimodal data.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs and MLLMs develop human-like object concept representations, as evidenced by low-dimensional embeddings derived from similarity judgments that are interpretable, show semantic clustering, and align with human neural activity patterns.
papers.conclusion: LLMs and MLLMs develop human-like conceptual representations of natural objects, with multimodal learning leading to more nuanced and brain-aligned representations.
papers.key_findings:
The derived 66-dimensional embeddings from LLM and MLLM similarity judgments are stable and predictive of both single-trial behavior and object similarity scores.
The embeddings exhibit spontaneous semantic clustering, mirroring human mental representations of object categories.
The dimensions underlying the embeddings are interpretable, reflecting semantic, perceptual, and spatial properties of objects.
There is a strong correspondence between the core dimensions identified in LLMs/MLLMs and those from human similarity judgments.
The model embeddings show strong alignment with neural activity patterns in functionally defined, category-selective brain regions (e.g., EBA, PPA, RSC, FFA).
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> The conceptualization and categorization of natural objects in the human mind have long intrigued cognitive scientists and neuroscientists, offering crucial insights into human perception and cognition. Recently, the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has raised the attractive question of whether these models can also develop human-like object representations through exposure to vast amounts of linguistic and multimodal data. In this study, we combined behavioral and neuroimaging analysis methods to uncover how the object concept representations in LLMs correlate with those of humans. By collecting large-scale datasets of 4.7 million triplet judgments from LLM and Multimodal LLM (MLLM), we were able to derive low-dimensional embeddings that capture the underlying similarity structure of 1,854 natural objects. The resulting 66-dimensional embeddings were found to be highly stable and predictive, and exhibited semantic clustering akin to human mental representations. Interestingly, the interpretability of the dimensions underlying these embeddings suggests that LLM and MLLM have developed human-like conceptual representations of natural objects. Further analysis demonstrated strong alignment between the identified model embeddings and neural activity patterns in many functionally defined brain ROIs (e.g., EBA, PPA, RSC and FFA). This provides compelling evidence that the object representations in LLMs, while not identical to those in the human, share fundamental commonalities that reflect key schemas of human conceptual knowledge. This study advances our understanding of machine intelligence and informs the development of more human-like artificial cognitive systems.

papers.title: How Deep is Love in LLMs' Hearts? Exploring Semantic Size in Human-like Cognition
papers.research_question: This study seeks to investigate whether LLMs exhibit similar tendencies in understanding semantic size as humans, thereby providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of human cognition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that multi-modal training is crucial for LLMs to achieve more human-like understanding of semantic size, and that LLMs, especially multi-modal ones, are influenced by attention-grabbing headlines with larger semantic size, revealing potential biases.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that multi-modal training enhances LLMs' understanding of semantic size, making them more human-like, but also introduces biases similar to humans, such as susceptibility to clickbait headlines.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-modal LLMs align more closely with human metaphorical tendencies compared to their text-only backbone LLMs.
Multi-modal LLMs outperform single-modality LLMs in semantic size classification accuracy, indicating multi-modality plays a critical role.
LLMs, especially MLLMs, show a clear preference for selecting product titles with larger semantic sizes in a controlled shopping scenario.
The findings suggest that human cognition cannot be fully acquired through the language modality alone; real-world, multi-modal experiences are essential.
Multi-modal training enhances LLMs' ability to understand both abstract and concrete concepts from a semantic size perspective.
papers.abstract: How human cognitive abilities are formed has long captivated researchers. However, a significant challenge lies in developing meaningful methods to measure these complex processes. With the advent of large language models (LLMs), which now rival human capabilities in various domains, we are presented with a unique testbed to investigate human cognition through a new lens. Among the many facets of cognition, one particularly crucial aspect is the concept of semantic size, the perceived magnitude of both abstract and concrete words or concepts. This study seeks to investigate whether LLMs exhibit similar tendencies in understanding semantic size, thereby providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of human cognition. We begin by exploring metaphorical reasoning, comparing how LLMs and humans associate abstract words with concrete objects of varying sizes. Next, we examine LLMs' internal representations to evaluate their alignment with human cognitive processes. Our findings reveal that multi-modal training is crucial for LLMs to achieve more human-like understanding, suggesting that real-world, multi-modal experiences are similarly vital for human cognitive development. Lastly, we examine whether LLMs are influenced by attention-grabbing headlines with larger semantic sizes in a real-world web shopping scenario. The results show that multi-modal LLMs are more emotionally engaged in decision-making, but this also introduces potential biases, such as the risk of manipulation through clickbait headlines. Ultimately, this study offers a novel perspective on how LLMs interpret and internalize language, from the smallest concrete objects to the most profound abstract concepts like love. The insights gained not only improve our understanding of LLMs but also provide new avenues for exploring the cognitive abilities that define human intelligence.

papers.title: Visualizing and Understanding Curriculum Learning for Long Short-Term Memory Networks
papers.research_question: How does curriculum learning affect the internal representations of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks?
papers.core_contribution: Curriculum learning, especially the baby step regimen, helps LSTM networks build more constructive internal representations (using previous timesteps as building blocks), improves performance for smaller models, and is more beneficial when training data is limited.
papers.conclusion: Curriculum learning helps LSTM construct partial sequence representations in a more intuitive way, enables smaller models to achieve better performance, and is particularly useful in low-resource training scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Curriculum learning biases LSTM models towards building constructive representations where internal states at previous timesteps are used as building blocks for the final prediction.
Smaller LSTM models show significant performance improvement when trained with curriculum learning.
Curriculum learning provides greater benefits when the amount of training data is limited.
The baby step curriculum regimen significantly improves LSTM performance on sentences with conjunctions in sentiment analysis.
Probing intermediate hidden states shows that the baby step curriculum leads to representations that correlate with the running sum in the digit sum task, unlike other regimens.
papers.abstract: Curriculum Learning emphasizes the order of training instances in a computational learning setup. The core hypothesis is that simpler instances should be learned early as building blocks to learn more complex ones. Despite its usefulness, it is still unknown how exactly the internal representation of models are affected by curriculum learning. In this paper, we study the effect of curriculum learning on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, which have shown strong competency in many Natural Language Processing (NLP) problems. Our experiments on sentiment analysis task and a synthetic task similar to sequence prediction tasks in NLP show that curriculum learning has a positive effect on the LSTM's internal states by biasing the model towards building constructive representations i.e. the internal representation at the previous timesteps are used as building blocks for the final prediction. We also find that smaller models significantly improves when they are trained with curriculum learning. Lastly, we show that curriculum learning helps more when the amount of training data is limited.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: On Semantic Cognition, Inductive Generalization, and Language Models
papers.research_question: What kinds of inductive generalizations about concepts are made by language models? To what extent do language models recognize and use emergent features during induction? How do the inductive generalization capacities of language models relate to their representational space?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an inductive reasoning-based framework to analyze semantic cognition and generalization in language models, drawing insights from cognitive science.
future_direction: Investigate inductive generalizations in language models
Study recognition and use of emergent features during induction
Analyze relationship between inductive generalization and representational space
papers.abstract: My doctoral research focuses on understanding semantic knowledge in neural network models trained solely to predict natural language (referred to as language models, or LMs), by drawing on insights from the study of concepts and categories grounded in cognitive science. I propose a framework inspired by 'inductive reasoning,' a phenomenon that sheds light on how humans utilize background knowledge to make inductive leaps and generalize from new pieces of information about concepts and their properties. Drawing from experiments that study inductive reasoning, I propose to analyze semantic inductive generalization in LMs using phenomena observed in human-induction literature, investigate inductive behavior on tasks such as implicit reasoning and emergent feature recognition, and analyze and relate induction dynamics to the learned conceptual representation space.

papers.title: Representation and Pre-Activation of Lexical-Semantic Knowledge in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How closely do the intermediate layers of LSTM and transformer language models correspond to human semantic knowledge, both before and after the target word is presented?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer models (GPT-2) are better at capturing semantic knowledge, especially attributive features, than LSTM models, and both models retain rich semantic representations of a concept after it has been presented.
papers.conclusion: The transformer model is much better at capturing attributive features than the LSTM model, whilst both models are able to retain rich semantic representations of the concept after the concept has been given to the network.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer models (GPT-2) outperform LSTM models in capturing semantic knowledge, particularly for attributive features.
Both models retain semantic information about a concept after the word is presented, with earlier layers performing better in the 'after' condition.
The final layer of both models shows a performance drop in the 'after' condition, likely due to increased context specificity.
In the 'before' condition (predicting the word), later layers are more representative of the upcoming word's semantics.
GPT-2's after representations are more effective in lower layers, while JLM's after representations are better in the first layer.
papers.limitation:
The feature pooling method may not fully capture context-specific representations, especially in later layers where representations become more context-specific.
Linear probes may not fully capture the information encoded in the representations; failure to decode a property does not mean it is not encoded.
papers.abstract: Neural network language models have the ability to capture the contextualised meanings of words in a sentence by dynamically evolving a representation of the linguistic input in a manner evocative of human language comprehension. While researchers have been able to analyse whether key linguistic regularities are adequately characterised by these evolving representations, determining whether they activate lexico-semantic knowledge similarly to humans remains challenging. In this paper, we perform a systematic analysis of how closely the intermediate layers from LSTM and transformer language models correspond to human semantic knowledge. Furthermore, in order to make more meaningful comparisons with theories of human language comprehension in psycholinguistics, we focus on two key stages where the meaning of a particular target word may arise: immediately before the word's presentation to the model (comparable to forward inferencing), and immediately after the word token has been input into the network. Our results indicate that the transformer models are better at capturing semantic knowledge relating to lexical concepts, both during word prediction and when retention is required.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: Discovering Hidden Visual Concepts Beyond Linguistic Input in Infant Learning
papers.research_question: Can a computational model trained on infant egocentric data acquire visual concepts that extend beyond its linguistic training vocabulary?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that infant-inspired models can develop visual concepts beyond their linguistic input and introduces NeuronClassifier, a training-free framework to discover and leverage these concepts for improved object recognition.
papers.conclusion: The work bridges cognitive science and computer vision by demonstrating that infant models develop visual concepts preceding linguistic input, similar to natural infant learning.
papers.key_findings:
CVCL contains visual concept neurons for objects not present in its training vocabulary, enabling out-of-vocabulary recognition.
NeuronClassifier outperforms the vanilla similarity-based method in in-vocabulary classification and enables out-of-vocabulary classification.
Out-of-vocabulary visual concepts tend to have higher Age of Acquisition ratings, aligning with infant development studies.
CVCL shares low-level feature representations with models like CLIP and ImageNet but diverges in higher-level features due to limited data diversity.
The framework reveals that models trained on infant data can form visual representations independently of linguistic supervision.
papers.limitation:
The study did not analyze the infant training data due to access constraints.
The analysis was not extended to adult egocentric data.
future_direction: Applying the NeuronClassifier framework to adult models and egocentric data.
papers.abstract: Infants develop complex visual understanding rapidly, even preceding the acquisition of linguistic skills. As computer vision seeks to replicate the human vision system, understanding infant visual development may offer valuable insights. In this paper, we present an interdisciplinary study exploring this question: can a computational model that imitates the infant learning process develop broader visual concepts that extend beyond the vocabulary it has heard, similar to how infants naturally learn? To investigate this, we analyze a recently published model in Science by Vong et al., which is trained on longitudinal, egocentric images of a single child paired with transcribed parental speech. We perform neuron labeling to identify visual concept neurons hidden in the model's internal representations. We then demonstrate that these neurons can recognize objects beyond the model's original vocabulary. Furthermore, we compare the differences in representation between infant models and those in modern computer vision models, such as CLIP and ImageNet pre-trained model. Ultimately, our work bridges cognitive science and computer vision by analyzing the internal representations of a computational model trained on an infant visual and linguistic inputs. Project page is available at https://kexueyi.github.io/webpage-discover-hidden-visual-concepts.

papers.title: N-Gram Learning and Pretraining Dynamics in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models acquire capabilities during pretraining, and what is the relationship between n-gram probabilities and this learning process?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation demonstrates a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning during pretraining, showing that language model learning is highly dependent on surface-level statistics and identifies bigram subnetworks as a minimal circuit for next token prediction.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning, suggesting that traditional distributional statistics still play a role in complex transformer models. Bigram subnetworks comprise a minimal subset of parameters necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn words differently from human children; word frequencies (unigram probabilities) account for the vast majority of variance in words' ages of acquisition in language models, but not in children.
Language model learning can be characterized as early n-gram learning for increasing n, followed by gradual refinement of low-probability n-gram predictions based on longer contexts and more nuanced capabilities.
Subnetworks that make bigram predictions exist in fully trained language models and are critical for model performance, even when they consist of less than 0.2% of model parameters.
Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer and overlap significantly with subnetworks trained to optimally prune a given model.
Bigram subnetworks recreate a pattern from the full models where the first layer induces a sharp change that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations.
papers.limitation:
Surprisal is an imperfect proxy for language model learning; a model might achieve the same surprisal at different points using different internal prediction strategies.
The work only considers language models with 124M parameters trained on 5.1B tokens, and learning curves may differ across model sizes.
future_direction: Further research is necessary to determine the effects of model size on learning speed, variability, and forgetting.
Characterize the examples (e.g., based on types of reasoning, world knowledge, or commonsense) that fluctuate at different points during pre-training across model sizes.
Bigram subnetworks can lay a foundation for studying more complex language model circuits by building up from a minimal circuit.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models have received unprecedented attention in recent years due to impressive performance on natural language tasks, but how they acquire these capabilities is largely unknown. During pretraining, language models are trained to predict next tokens (e.g. words) in text, and the field of pretraining dynamics aims to demonstrate how this learning objective leads to consistent learning patterns and mechanisms. The primary contributions of this dissertation are to demonstrate relationships between n-gram probabilities (next token predictions based only on the previous n-1 tokens) and language model learning during pretraining. I first show that language models learn words differently from human children; word frequencies (unigram probabilities) account for the vast majority of variance in words’ ages of acquisition in language models, but not in children. I then characterize language model learning as early n-gram learning for increasing n, then gradual refinement of low probability n-gram predictions based on longer contexts and more nuanced capabilities. Mechanistically, subnetworks that make bigram predictions exist in the models long after the full models have moved on from simple bigram predictions. These bigram subnetworks are critical to language modeling performance even in fully trained models, and they recreate several key properties of a language model’s activation space across layers. Together, these results demonstrate a close relationship between n-gram probabilities and language model learning, suggesting that traditional distributional statistics still play some role in these more complex models.

papers.title: Relational Schemata in BERT Are Inducible, Not Emergent: A Study of Performance vs. Competence in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does BERT encode abstract relational schemata, and is relational abstraction emergent from pretraining or induced via task scaffolding?
papers.core_contribution: Relational schemata in BERT are not emergent from pretraining but can be induced through task-specific fine-tuning, revealing a performance-competence gap where high classification accuracy does not imply structured internal representations.
papers.conclusion: This study demonstrates a clear separation between performance and competence in BERT's handling of relational reasoning. Relational abstraction is not an emergent property of pretraining but must be actively induced through guided learning.
papers.key_findings:
Pretrained BERT achieves high accuracy (79%) on relation classification, but its internal representations do not show relational structure (low RSA correlation).
After fine-tuning, BERT's accuracy increases to 90% and its internal representations show strong relational structure (high RSA correlation and clustering in embedding space).
A performance-competence gap exists: BERT can perform well on relational tasks without having structured internal representations.
Relational abstraction is not emergent from pretraining but requires task-specific supervision to induce.
Control experiments with randomized labels confirm that classification success and RSA structure reflect genuine relational signals, not dataset artifacts.
future_direction: Explore whether similar patterns of inducibility extend to other language models (e.g., LLaMa, Gemma) and whether model scale influences the emergence of relational structure.
Extend the range of tested relations to include temporal or causal relations.
Bridge insights from cognitive development (e.g., curriculum learning, relational priming) to inspire new training paradigms.
papers.abstract: While large language models like BERT demonstrate strong empirical performance on semantic tasks, whether this reflects true conceptual competence or surface-level statistical association remains unclear. I investigate whether BERT encodes abstract relational schemata by examining internal representations of concept pairs across taxonomic, mereological, and functional relations. I compare BERT's relational classification performance with representational structure in [CLS] token embeddings. Results reveal that pretrained BERT enables high classification accuracy, indicating latent relational signals. However, concept pairs organize by relation type in high-dimensional embedding space only after fine-tuning on supervised relation classification tasks. This indicates relational schemata are not emergent from pretraining alone but can be induced via task scaffolding. These findings demonstrate that behavioral performance does not necessarily imply structured conceptual understanding, though models can acquire inductive biases for grounded relational abstraction through appropriate training.

papers.title: Emergence of Hidden Capabilities: Exploring Learning Dynamics in Concept Space
papers.research_question: What determines the concepts a model learns, the order in which it learns them, and its ability to manipulate those concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept space framework to analyze learning dynamics, showing that concept signal controls learning speed and order, and that hidden capabilities emerge suddenly during training before they can be elicited by naive prompting.
papers.conclusion: Generative models possess hidden capabilities that are learned suddenly and consistently during training, but naive input prompting may not elicit these capabilities, hence hiding how competent the model actually is.
papers.key_findings:
Concept signal (sensitivity of data-generating process to a concept) determines the speed at which a concept is learned.
Learning dynamics in concept space show sudden turns that correspond to the emergence of hidden capabilities.
Hidden capabilities (ability to generate out-of-distribution concept classes) can be elicited via latent interventions before they are accessible via naive prompting.
papers.limitation: The experiments are conducted on toy datasets and simple models, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex models and datasets.
Investigating the role of architecture and training objectives in concept learning.
papers.abstract: Modern generative models demonstrate impressive capabilities, likely stemming from an ability to identify and manipulate abstract concepts underlying their training data. However, fundamental questions remain: what determines the concepts a model learns, the order in which it learns them, and its ability to manipulate those concepts? To address these questions, we propose analyzing a model's learning dynamics via a framework we call the concept space, where each axis represents an independent concept underlying the data generating process. By characterizing learning dynamics in this space, we identify how the speed at which a concept is learned, and hence the order of concept learning, is controlled by properties of the data we term concept signal. Further, we observe moments of sudden turns in the direction of a model's learning dynamics in concept space. Surprisingly, these points precisely correspond to the emergence of hidden capabilities, i.e., where latent interventions show the model possesses the capability to manipulate a concept, but these capabilities cannot yet be elicited via naive input prompting. While our results focus on synthetically defined toy datasets, we hypothesize a general claim on emergence of hidden capabilities may hold: generative models possess latent capabilities that emerge suddenly and consistently during training, though a model might not exhibit these capabilities under naive input prompting.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Crosscoding Through Time: Tracking Emergence & Consolidation Of Linguistic Representations Throughout LLM Pretraining
papers.research_question: How do linguistic features emerge and evolve during the pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using sparse crosscoders and the Relative Indirect Effect (RELIE) metric to track the emergence and evolution of linguistic features during LLM pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The approach is architecture-agnostic and scalable, offering a promising path toward more interpretable and fine-grained analysis of representation learning throughout pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Crosscoders can detect feature emergence, maintenance, and discontinuation during pretraining.
Features evolve from token-specific detectors to abstract syntactic concepts over training time.
The Relative Indirect Effect (RELIE) metric effectively traces the causal importance of features across checkpoints.
The method is architecture-agnostic and scalable to billion-parameter models.
Multilingual models develop cross-lingual feature sharing, with abstract concepts becoming more universal over time.
papers.limitation: Early checkpoints may resist sparse mapping and accurate reconstruction with crosscoders.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) learn non-trivial abstractions during pretraining, like detecting irregular plural noun subjects. However, it is not well understood when and how specific linguistic abilities emerge as traditional evaluation methods such as benchmarking fail to reveal how models acquire concepts and capabilities. To bridge this gap and better understand model training at the concept level, we use sparse crosscoders to discover and align features across model checkpoints. Using this approach, we track the evolution of linguistic features during pretraining. We train crosscoders between open-sourced checkpoint triplets with significant performance and representation shifts, and introduce a novel metric, Relative Indirect Effects (RelIE), to trace training stages at which individual features become causally important for task performance. We show that crosscoders can detect feature emergence, maintenance, and discontinuation during pretraining. Our approach is architecture-agnostic and scalable, offering a promising path toward more interpretable and fine-grained analysis of representation learning throughout pretraining.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts across modalities
papers.research_question: Do language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across different input modalities (text and images)?
papers.core_contribution: Language models predict brain activity better in regions with high semantic consistency across modalities, even when those regions are not language-selective, suggesting LMs develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.conclusion: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across modalities, indicating that LMs may internally develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.key_findings:
Brain regions with higher semantic consistency (responding similarly to concepts across text and image paradigms) are better predicted by LM representations.
This correlation holds even in brain regions with weak language selectivity.
Representational similarity between LMs and semantically consistent brain regions is significant and increases for vision-language models when using both text and image stimuli.
Both language-only and vision-language models show alignment with semantically consistent brain regions.
papers.limitation:
The picture paradigm correlation is lower and skewed by visual cortex areas that encode images but not necessarily concepts.
The study uses an inter-participant noise ceiling due to lack of repeated trials, which may not capture all variability.
papers.abstract: Cognitive science and neuroscience have long faced the challenge of disentangling representations of language from representations of conceptual meaning. As the same problem arises in today's language models (LMs), we investigate the relationship between LM--brain alignment and two neural metrics: (1) the level of brain activation during processing of sentences, targeting linguistic processing, and (2) a novel measure of meaning consistency across input modalities, which quantifies how consistently a brain region responds to the same concept across paradigms (sentence, word cloud, image) using an fMRI dataset (Pereira et al., 2018). Our experiments show that both language-only and language-vision models predict the signal better in more meaning-consistent areas of the brain, even when these areas are not strongly sensitive to language processing, suggesting that LMs might internally represent cross-modal conceptual meaning.

papers.title: Probing Across Time: What Does RoBERTa Know and When?
papers.research_question: For various types of knowledge a language model learns, when during (pre)training are they acquired?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing across time framework and finds that during pretraining, linguistic knowledge is acquired fast and stably, factual and commonsense knowledge slower and more domain-sensitive, and reasoning abilities are largely not stably acquired.
papers.conclusion: RoBERTa learns linguistic knowledge faster than factual and commonsense knowledge, but struggles to learn reasoning abilities. The probing across time framework can serve as a general framework to inform progress on models and probes.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic knowledge is acquired fast, stably, and robustly across domains.
Factual and commonsense knowledge are acquired slower and are more domain-sensitive.
Reasoning abilities are largely not stably acquired.
The learning order and patterns hold regardless of data variation (domain and size), but domain diversity is more important than quantity.
Benchmark tasks that require complex knowledge (e.g., ReCoRD, WSC) benefit from longer pretraining, aligning with probing results.
papers.limitation:
Changes to hyperparameters might lead to different conclusions.
Differences in pretraining setup (e.g., batch size, data) may cause performance degradation compared to original RoBERTa.
future_direction: Exploration of different objectives and architectures (e.g., GPT-2).
More efficient pretraining by understanding when necessary knowledge is acquired.
Understanding dependencies among different kinds of knowledge.
papers.abstract: Models of language trained on very large corpora have been demonstrated useful for NLP. As fixed artifacts, they have become the object of intense study, with many researchers "probing" the extent to which linguistic abstractions, factual and commonsense knowledge, and reasoning abilities they acquire and readily demonstrate. Building on this line of work, we consider a new question: for types of knowledge a language model learns, when during (pre)training are they acquired? We plot probing performance across iterations, using RoBERTa as a case study. Among our findings: linguistic knowledge is acquired fast, stably, and robustly across domains. Facts and commonsense are slower and more domain-sensitive. Reasoning abilities are, in general, not stably acquired. As new datasets, pretraining protocols, and probes emerge, we believe that probing-across-time analyses can help researchers understand the complex, intermingled learning that these models undergo and guide us toward more efficient approaches that accomplish necessary learning faster.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
