The brain regions of interest (ROIs) considered may not capture all regions involved in multimodal integration.
Averaging brain responses across participants may smooth out participant-specific patterns.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that transformer-based vision-language models (VLMs) capture the multimodality of concept processing in the human brain. However, a systematic evaluation exploring different types of VLM architectures and the role played by visual and textual context is still lacking. Here, we analyse multiple VLMs employing different strategies to integrate visual and textual modalities, along with language-only counterparts. We measure the alignment between concept representations by models and existing (fMRI) brain responses to concept words presented in two experimental conditions, where either visual (pictures) or textual (sentences) context is provided. Our results reveal that VLMs outperform the language-only counterparts in both experimental conditions. However, controlled ablation studies show that only for some VLMs, such as LXMERT and IDEFICS2, brain alignment stems from genuinely learning more human-like concepts during pretraining, while others are highly sensitive to the context provided at inference. Additionally, we find that vision-language encoders are more brain-aligned than more recent, generative VLMs. Altogether, our study shows that VLMs align with human neural representations in concept processing, while highlighting differences among architectures. We open-source code and materials to reproduce our experiments at: https://github.com/dmg-illc/vl-concept-processing.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Model Organisms for Human Associative Learning
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit representational dynamics akin to human associative learning, and can they help disambiguate between competing hypotheses for representational change? How does vocabulary interference modulate representational change?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit a non-monotonic pattern of representational change during associative learning (consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis), and this change is modulated by vocabulary interference, with higher interference leading to stronger differentiation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can serve as accessible and general computational models for studying human associative learning, providing new insights into how local pair similarity and global competition shape representational change.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show three distinct phases of learning during in-context associative learning: encoding (accuracy increases), consolidation (accuracy stabilizes), and forgetting (accuracy declines).
During the consolidation phase, moderately similar token pairs significantly differentiate, producing a U-shaped pattern of representational change that aligns with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis.
Vocabulary interference—the similarity between a paired item and the model's prior knowledge—modulates representational change: higher interference leads to stronger differentiation.
The non-monotonic differentiation pattern is only present during consolidation and disappears during encoding and forgetting phases.
These representational dynamics are consistent across six different open-source LLMs, despite architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
The token pairs used are synthetic and optimized for similarity, which may not reflect naturalistic learning scenarios.
The forgetting phase is not well understood, and its causes require further investigation.
LLMs are not biologically plausible models of the brain, limiting direct comparisons to neural mechanisms.
future_direction: Investigating the causes of forgetting and predicting when it occurs.
Extending the analysis to more naturalistic stimuli and real-world associative learning tasks.
Exploring how different model architectures (e.g., with explicit memory modules) affect representational dynamics.
papers.abstract: Associative learning--forming links between co-occurring items--is fundamental to human cognition, reshaping internal representations in complex ways. Testing hypotheses on how representational changes occur in biological systems is challenging, but large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative. Building on LLMs' in-context learning, we adapt a cognitive neuroscience associative learning paradigm and investigate how representations evolve across six models. Our initial findings reveal a non-monotonic pattern consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis, with moderately similar items differentiating after learning. Leveraging the controllability of LLMs, we further show that this differentiation is modulated by the overlap of associated items with the broader vocabulary--a factor we term vocabulary interference, capturing how new associations compete with prior knowledge. We find that higher vocabulary interference amplifies differentiation, suggesting that representational change is influenced by both item similarity and global competition. Our findings position LLMs not only as powerful tools for studying representational dynamics in human-like learning systems, but also as accessible and general computational models for generating new hypotheses about the principles underlying memory reorganization in the brain.

papers.title: Insights on Neural Representations for End-to-End Speech Recognition
papers.research_question: How do neural representations correlate across layers and training in end-to-end ASR models, and how does this relate to model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides insights into hierarchical correlation dependencies in CNN layers, bottom-up patterns in LSTM, and irregular correlations in Transformer layers for end-to-end ASR, showing how CCA and CKA can analyze neural representations and identify pathological components.
papers.conclusion: A comparative analysis of SVCCA and CKA identified pathological components in CNN and Transformer models, and these techniques can be used to gain insights into neural representations for building better ASR models.
papers.key_findings:
CNN layers exhibit hierarchical correlation dependencies as layer depth increases.
LSTM architecture shows a bottom-up pattern across the training process.
Transformer encoder layers exhibit irregular correlation as neural depth increases.
SVCCA is more sensitive to initialization parameters and under-represents neural representations compared to CKA.
CKA can visualize pathology in neural representations during training, especially in Transformer models.
papers.limitation:
SVCCA's SVD component relies on the reflection of class information, which is a potential limitation for end-to-end speech recognition.
CKA has high computational costs for large models due to size and computational requirements.
future_direction: Compare correlation of trained neural layers across different speech datasets, such as noisy or augmented data.
Analyze neural representations on out-of-domain data.
Explore few-shot-learning in ASR using these insights.
papers.abstract:
End-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) models aim to learn a
generalised speech representation. However, there are limited tools available
to understand the internal functions and the effect of hierarchical
dependencies within the model architecture. It is crucial to understand the
correlations between the layer-wise representations, to derive insights on the
relationship between neural representations and performance.
 Previous investigations of network similarities using correlation analysis
techniques have not been explored for End-to-End ASR models. This paper
analyses and explores the internal dynamics between layers during training with
CNN, LSTM and Transformer based approaches using Canonical correlation analysis
(CCA) and centered kernel alignment (CKA) for the experiments. It was found
that neural representations within CNN layers exhibit hierarchical correlation
dependencies as layer depth increases but this is mostly limited to cases where
neural representation correlates more closely. This behaviour is not observed
in LSTM architecture, however there is a bottom-up pattern observed across the
training process, while Transformer encoder layers exhibit irregular
coefficiency correlation as neural depth increases. Altogether, these results
provide new insights into the role that neural architectures have upon speech
recognition performance. More specifically, these techniques can be used as
indicators to build better performing speech recognition models.

papers.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
papers.research_question: Can editing representations, instead of weights, be a more powerful alternative for parameter-efficient finetuning of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representation Finetuning (ReFT), a family of parameter-efficient finetuning methods that edit hidden representations instead of weights, and shows that it is more parameter-efficient and often outperforms existing PEFTs.
papers.conclusion: ReFT methods are a promising alternative to weight-based PEFTs, offering a better balance of efficiency and performance, and are worthy of further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
ReFT methods are 15×–65× more parameter-efficient than LoRA.
LoReFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on commonsense reasoning, instruction-following, and natural language understanding.
ReFT methods are less effective on arithmetic reasoning tasks, possibly due to the length of chain-of-thought generations.
ReFT performance scales with model size.
LoReFT outperforms full finetuning on instruction-following with only 0.0039% of parameters.
papers.limitation: ReFTs may have trouble with chain-of-thought reasoning tasks due to the length of generations and overall greater difficulty of the task.
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods seek to adapt large neural models via updates to a small number of weights. However, much prior interpretability work has shown that representations encode rich semantic information, suggesting that editing representations might be a more powerful alternative. We pursue this hypothesis by developing a family of Representation Finetuning (ReFT) methods. ReFT methods operate on a frozen base model and learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations. We define a strong instance of the ReFT family, Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT), and we identify an ablation of this method that trades some performance for increased efficiency. Both are drop-in replacements for existing PEFTs and learn interventions that are 15x--65x more parameter-efficient than LoRA. We showcase LoReFT on eight commonsense reasoning tasks, four arithmetic reasoning tasks, instruction-tuning, and GLUE. In all these evaluations, our ReFTs deliver the best balance of efficiency and performance, and almost always outperform state-of-the-art PEFTs. We release a generic ReFT training library publicly at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: LLMs model how humans induce logically structured rules
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) model human induction of logically structured rules? Do they provide a good fit to human behavior and do they use similar logical or logic-like operators?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can model human logical rule induction as well as Bayesian probabilistic Language of Thought (pLoT) models, and they may instantiate a novel theoretical account of human logical concepts without built-in logical primitives.
papers.conclusion: LLMs provide a good model of human logical rule induction and may offer a new theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations underlying human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.
papers.key_findings:
Some LLMs (e.g., GPT4, Gemma-7b) achieve human-level accuracy on logical rule induction tasks.
When prompted to explain rules, LLMs sometimes produce rules that use logical operators similar to humans.
Tuning an LLM (Gemma-7b) on human responses yields a better fit to human learning trajectories than tuning on correct answers or than Bayesian pLoT models.
The tuned LLM's high correlation with human data is not just due to learning the rules correctly; it captures human-like learning patterns.
The tuning generalizes to held-out rules and to new rule types (e.g., minority/majority judgments).
papers.limitation:
It is hard to know what the LLM learns when tuning to human responses, and it is hard to fully eliminate the concern that the tuning process is introducing an artifact that increases fit even on withheld exemplars.
The held-out rules share components with seen rules, so generalization might not be fully compositional.
future_direction: Investigate the representations and processes LLMs use for logical rule induction.
Compare LLM-based accounts to human cognitive processes more deeply.
papers.abstract: A central goal of cognitive science is to provide a computationally explicit account of both the structure of the mind and its development: what are the primitive representational building blocks of cognition, what are the rules via which those primitives combine, and where do these primitives and rules come from in the first place? A long-standing debate concerns the adequacy of artificial neural networks as computational models that can answer these questions, in particular in domains related to abstract cognitive function, such as language and logic. This paper argues that recent advances in neural networks -- specifically, the advent of large language models (LLMs) -- represent an important shift in this debate. We test a variety of LLMs on an existing experimental paradigm used for studying the induction of rules formulated over logical concepts. Across four experiments, we find converging empirical evidence that LLMs provide at least as good a fit to human behavior as models that implement a Bayesian probablistic language of thought (pLoT), which have been the best computational models of human behavior on the same task. Moreover, we show that the LLMs make qualitatively different predictions about the nature of the rules that are inferred and deployed in order to complete the task, indicating that the LLM is unlikely to be a mere implementation of the pLoT solution. Based on these results, we argue that LLMs may instantiate a novel theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations necessary to explain human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Investigating word learning processes in an artificial agent
papers.research_question: How can we analyze the internal representations of a computational word-learning model to assess its cognitive plausibility and relate it to infant word learning?
papers.core_contribution: Develops novel quantitative methods to analyze internal representations of a computational word-learning model and discusses their ecological validity for child language acquisition.
papers.conclusion: It is difficult to examine computational models in detail and relate them to infant learning, emphasizing the need for tools to inspect internal workings.
papers.key_findings:
The model quickly forms one-to-one associations between keywords and acoustic patterns, and these associations stabilize early.
The model's internal representations continue to evolve even after accuracy plateaus, with updates occurring upon encountering new instances of keywords.
Speaker changes induce stronger updates in keyword columns compared to same-speaker repetitions, indicating sensitivity to speaker characteristics.
Non-keyword columns are necessary for accurate recognition but do not encode interpretable high-level linguistic features.
The model does not develop speaker-dependent representations, likely due to the orthogonal coding of conceptual information.
papers.limitation:
The orthogonal pseudo-visual coding strongly biases the model's internal organization, making more sophisticated representations unlikely to emerge.
The strong binding of acoustic and conceptual information early in training may stem from the orthogonality of the encoding rather than a general learning principle.
future_direction: Further investigation into the impact of conceptual coding schemes on model behavior.
Development of tools to enable detailed inspection of computational models.
papers.abstract: Researchers in human language processing and acquisition are making an increasing use of computational models. Computer simulations provide a valuable platform to reproduce hypothesised learning mechanisms that are otherwise very difficult, if not impossible, to verify on human subjects. However, computational models come with problems and risks. It is difficult to (automatically) extract essential information about the developing internal representations from a set of simulation runs, and often researchers limit themselves to analysing learning curves based on empirical recognition accuracy through time. The associated risk is to erroneously deem a specific learning behaviour as generalisable to human learners, while it could also be a mere consequence (artifact) of the implementation of the artificial learner or of the input coding scheme. In this paper a set of simulation runs taken from the ACORNS project is investigated. First a look `inside the box' of the learner is provided by employing novel quantitative methods for analysing changing structures in large data sets. Then, the obtained findings are discussed in the perspective of their ecological validity in the field of child language acquisition.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how LLMs develop causally functional representations of semantic roles, specifically focusing on the localization, emergence dynamics, and cross-scale/cross-family generalization of semantic-role circuits.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a causal-temporal method for discovering and tracking semantic-role circuits in LLMs, and finds that these circuits are highly localized, emerge via gradual refinement, and show partial transfer across scales and architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure that exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures, suggesting that transformers encode predicate-argument binding via compact circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic-role information is encoded in compact, role-specific circuits (89–92% attribution within ≤20 nodes).
These circuits emerge via continuous refinement rather than discrete phase transitions.
There is a structure-function dissociation: circuits stabilize structurally before becoming functionally indispensable.
Cross-scale and cross-family analysis shows moderate component reuse (24–51% node overlap) but divergent wiring.
Larger models reuse similar components while rewiring connections.
papers.abstract: Despite displaying semantic competence, large language models' internal mechanisms that ground abstract semantic structure remain insufficiently characterised. We propose a method integrating role-cross minimal pairs, temporal emergence analysis, and cross-model comparison to study how LLMs implement semantic roles. Our analysis uncovers: (i) highly concentrated circuits (89-94% attribution within 28 nodes); (ii) gradual structural refinement rather than phase transitions, with larger models sometimes bypassing localised circuits; and (iii) moderate cross-scale conservation (24-59% component overlap) alongside high spectral similarity. These findings suggest that LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure, and these mechanisms exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do features in language models emerge and evolve internally during pre-training? What is the internal dynamics of model pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using cross-snapshot crosscoders to track the evolution of interpretable features during language model pre-training, revealing a two-phase learning process (statistical then feature learning) and establishing causal connections between feature formation and downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that cross-snapshot crosscoders can successfully track fine-grained feature evolution during pre-training, providing empirical evidence for a statistical-to-feature-learning phase transition and opening possibilities for detailed analysis of representation learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Feature evolution follows a two-phase pattern: a statistical learning phase followed by a feature learning phase, with most features beginning to form around step 1000.
Decoder norms of crosscoder features serve as effective proxies for tracking feature strength and presence across training snapshots.
More complex features (e.g., induction, context-sensitive) tend to emerge later in training than simpler features (e.g., previous token).
Attribution-based circuit tracing shows that the formation of specific crosscoder features causally contributes to improvements on downstream tasks like subject-verb agreement.
Features undergo a universal directional shift around step 1000, after which they rotate more gradually while maintaining similarity to their post-step 1000 orientations.
papers.limitation: Crosscoders may theoretically misalign unrelated features or split shared features across snapshots, though the authors argue these are rare in practice.
papers.abstract: Language models obtain extensive capabilities through pre-training. However, the pre-training process remains a black box. In this work, we track linear interpretable feature evolution across pre-training snapshots using a sparse dictionary learning method called crosscoders. We find that most features begin to form around a specific point, while more complex patterns emerge in later training stages. Feature attribution analyses reveal causal connections between feature evolution and downstream performance. Our feature-level observations are highly consistent with previous findings on Transformer's two-stage learning process, which we term a statistical learning phase and a feature learning phase. Our work opens up the possibility to track fine-grained representation progress during language model learning dynamics.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Vocabulary embeddings organize linguistic structure early in language model training
papers.research_question: How are the input vocabulary representations of language models structured, and how and when does this structure evolve over training?
papers.core_contribution: Vocabulary embeddings quickly converge to high correlations with semantic and syntactic features during training, with high-frequency and function words converging faster than low-frequency words, which retain alignment with their random initializations.
papers.conclusion: Vocabulary embeddings rapidly organize linguistic structure early in training, with frequency and function playing distinct roles, motivating deeper study of how embedding evolution facilitates capability gains.
papers.key_findings:
During training, vocabulary embedding geometry quickly converges to high correlations with semantic and syntactic features.
Embeddings of high-frequency and function words converge to their final vectors faster than lexical and low-frequency words.
Low-frequency words retain some alignment with the bias in their random initializations, while high-frequency words completely shed initialization biases.
Embeddings continue to change after linguistic features stabilize, with rare words moving closer to their morphological inflections.
The correlation between input and output embeddings peaks when linguistic features stabilize.
future_direction: Understanding why OLMo attains stronger part-of-speech correlations than Pythia.
Understanding the interactions of combined linguistic features in model embeddings.
Understanding the dynamics and geometry of subword tokens.
Studying how the evolution of vocabulary geometry may facilitate specific capability gains during model training.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) work by manipulating the geometry of input embedding vectors over multiple layers. Here, we ask: how are the input vocabulary representations of language models structured, and how and when does this structure evolve over training? To answer this question, we use representational similarity analysis, running a suite of experiments that correlate the geometric structure of the input embeddings and output embeddings of two open-source models (Pythia 12B and OLMo 7B) with semantic, syntactic, and frequency-based metrics over the course of training. Our key findings are as follows: 1) During training, the vocabulary embedding geometry quickly converges to high correlations with a suite of semantic and syntactic features; 2) Embeddings of high-frequency and function words (e.g., "the," "of") converge to their final vectors faster than lexical and low-frequency words, which retain some alignment with the bias in their random initializations. These findings help map the dynamic trajectory by which input embeddings organize around linguistic structure, revealing distinct roles for word frequency and function. Our findings motivate a deeper study of how the evolution of vocabulary geometry may facilitate specific capability gains during model training.

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression: From Language-Specific to Shared Neurons
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models achieve cross-lingual generalization? The paper investigates the connection between cross-lingual generalization and compression during pre-training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides empirical evidence that cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, with representations evolving from language-specific to shared, cross-lingual abstractions, observable in the alignment of concept-specific neurons.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models is driven by compression during pre-training, leading to shared neural representations for concepts across languages, independent of the original language encoding.
papers.key_findings:
During pre-training, model representations evolve from language-specific to cross-lingual abstractions, consistent with a compression effect.
Language identification probing shows a shift from uniform capabilities across layers to specialized layer functions, with middle layers becoming more language-agnostic.
Specific neurons become increasingly aligned across languages for the same semantic concepts as training progresses.
Manipulating concept-specific neurons identified in one language can guide semantically coherent text generation in another language, demonstrating shared neural representations.
papers.limitation:
The number of available training checkpoints for the BLOOM models is limited.
The concept dataset is created by machine translation, which may introduce noise and errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to transfer knowledge across languages, despite being trained without explicit cross-lingual supervision. We analyze the parameter spaces of three MLLMs to study how their representations evolve during pre-training, observing patterns consistent with compression: models initially form language-specific representations, which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses. Through probing experiments, we observe a clear transition from uniform language identification capabilities across layers to more specialized layer functions. For deeper analysis, we focus on neurons that encode distinct semantic concepts. By tracing their development during pre-training, we show how they gradually align across languages. Notably, we identify specific neurons that emerge as increasingly reliable predictors for the same concepts across languages.

papers.title: Analogs of Linguistic Structure in Deep Representations
papers.research_question: Does the compositional structure of natural language, such as negation and coordination, spontaneously arise in neural representations trained on a communication game without language supervision?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neural representations trained on a communication game without language data develop compositional structure analogous to natural language, including linear transformations corresponding to negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that neural representations can develop compositional structure analogous to natural language, and highlights the value of formal semantics for interpreting deep models.
papers.key_findings:
Human-produced referring expressions are highly predictive of RNN model behavior, with 90% object-level agreement.
A linear transformation of message vectors robustly corresponds to logical negation, with 97% object-level agreement.
Linear transformations for conjunction and disjunction show some correspondence but are less precise than for negation.
The RNN model spontaneously develops representations with compositional structure similar to natural language syntax.
The space of neural representations exhibits geometric regularities analogous to logical operations.
papers.limitation:
Linear transformations for conjunction and disjunction are less precise and not everywhere well approximated as linear.
The analysis does not address hierarchical application of multiple transformations.
future_direction: exploring recursive structure in neural representations
papers.abstract: We investigate the compositional structure of message vectors computed by a deep network trained on a communication game. By comparing truth-conditional representations of encoder-produced message vectors to human-produced referring expressions, we are able to identify aligned (vector, utterance) pairs with the same meaning. We then search for structured relationships among these aligned pairs to discover simple vector space transformations corresponding to negation, conjunction, and disjunction. Our results suggest that neural representations are capable of spontaneously developing a "syntax" with functional analogues to qualitative properties of natural language.

papers.title: On Linear Representations and Pretraining Data Frequency in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the connection between pretraining data frequency and the formation of linear representations of factual relations in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The formation of linear representations for factual recall in language models is strongly correlated with pretraining term frequencies, and measuring these representations allows prediction of term frequencies in the pretraining corpus.
papers.conclusion: Linear representations of factual triplets in LMs are connected to pretraining frequencies, which can guide interpretability work and enable prediction of term frequencies in closed-data models.
papers.key_findings:
The development of linear representations for factual recall relations in LMs is related to frequency as well as model size.
Linear representations form at predictable frequency thresholds during training, regardless of when this threshold is met, and correlate strongly with recall accuracy.
Measuring the extent to which a relation is represented linearly allows prediction of the approximate frequencies of individual terms in the pretraining corpus, even without access to the training data.
The predictive signal from linear representations is stronger than that from log probabilities and task accuracies alone.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on factual relations and leaves non-factual relations (e.g., gender stereotypes) for future work.
The regression model provides approximate frequency predictions within bounds, not exact counts.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to non-factual relations.
Improve the bounds of predicted frequencies.
Understand if and when LMs use non-linear methods to solve tasks.
papers.abstract: Pretraining data has a direct impact on the behaviors and quality of language models (LMs), but we only understand the most basic principles of this relationship. While most work focuses on pretraining data's effect on downstream task behavior, we investigate its relationship to LM representations. Previous work has discovered that, in language models, some concepts are encoded `linearly' in the representations, but what factors cause these representations to form? We study the connection between pretraining data frequency and models' linear representations of factual relations. We find evidence that the formation of linear representations is strongly connected to pretraining term frequencies; specifically for subject-relation-object fact triplets, both subject-object co-occurrence frequency and in-context learning accuracy for the relation are highly correlated with linear representations. This is the case across all phases of pretraining. In OLMo-7B and GPT-J, we discover that a linear representation consistently (but not exclusively) forms when the subjects and objects within a relation co-occur at least 1k and 2k times, respectively, regardless of when these occurrences happen during pretraining. Finally, we train a regression model on measurements of linear representation quality in fully-trained LMs that can predict how often a term was seen in pretraining. Our model achieves low error even on inputs from a different model with a different pretraining dataset, providing a new method for estimating properties of the otherwise-unknown training data of closed-data models. We conclude that the strength of linear representations in LMs contains signal about the models' pretraining corpora that may provide new avenues for controlling and improving model behavior: particularly, manipulating the models' training data to meet specific frequency thresholds.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Is neural language acquisition similar to natural? A chronological probing study
papers.research_question: Is neural language acquisition in transformer models similar to natural language acquisition in humans? Specifically, how do language models acquire linguistic structures during training and in what order?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces chronological probing, a methodology to analyze how language models acquire linguistic structures during training, and finds that linguistic information is acquired early and in a specific order, with discourse being harder to learn.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models acquire morphological and syntactic features early in training, but discourse features are not fully acquired, and models do not surpass the language proficiency of an 8-year-old child in discourse tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic information is acquired in the early stages of training (before 600,000 iterations).
Both MultiBERT and T5 capture features from various language levels (morphology, syntax, discourse) but can inconsistently fail on tasks perceived as easy.
Discourse tasks are acquired more slowly and to a lesser extent compared to morphology and syntax.
The acquisition order and trajectory are similar across the two different model architectures (MultiBERT and T5).
Models do not reach the discourse proficiency level of an 8-year-old child.
papers.limitation:
T5 does not give results on BLiMP due to its generation algorithm, limiting the comparison of syntactic and morphological acquisition across models.
Some tasks (e.g., Discourse Coherence and Person) are performed with quality similar to embeddings with shuffled labels, indicating difficulty with certain discourse tasks.
future_direction: Adaptation of the BLiMP dataset for T5 architecture is left for further research.
The authors welcome the community to reproduce the experimental setup and apply the chronological probing approach to other architectures.
papers.abstract: The probing methodology allows one to obtain a partial representation of linguistic phenomena stored in the inner layers of the neural network, using external classifiers and statistical analysis. Pre-trained transformer-based language models are widely used both for natural language understanding (NLU) and natural language generation (NLG) tasks making them most commonly used for downstream applications. However, little analysis was carried out, whether the models were pre-trained enough or contained knowledge correlated with linguistic theory. We are presenting the chronological probing study of transformer English models such as MultiBERT and T5. We sequentially compare the information about the language learned by the models in the process of training on corpora. The results show that 1) linguistic information is acquired in the early stages of training 2) both language models demonstrate capabilities to capture various features from various levels of language, including morphology, syntax, and even discourse, while they also can inconsistently fail on tasks that are perceived as easy. We also introduce the open-source framework for chronological probing research, compatible with other transformer-based models. https://github.com/EkaterinaVoloshina/chronological_probing

papers.title: Optimizing Rank for High-Fidelity Implicit Neural Representations
papers.research_question: Does the low-frequency bias of vanilla MLPs in implicit neural representations stem from an intrinsic architectural limitation or from rank degradation during training? How can optimization strategies that preserve rank improve INR fidelity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the low-frequency bias of vanilla MLPs in implicit neural representations is due to rank degradation during training, and that using an orthogonalizing optimizer (Muon) to preserve rank can significantly improve the fidelity of INRs across various architectures and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Optimization and rank preservation are crucial for the performance of implicit neural representations, and orthogonalizing optimizers like Muon can significantly improve fidelity, challenging the prevailing focus on architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
Stable rank degradation during training is the primary cause of the low-frequency bias in vanilla MLPs for implicit neural representations.
Orthogonalizing optimizers like Muon, which enforce high-rank, near-orthogonal weight updates, can preserve rank and enable even simple MLPs to achieve high-fidelity reconstructions.
Muon consistently improves performance across a wide range of INR architectures (ReLU MLP, FFN, Gaussian, SIREN, WIRE, FINER) and tasks (image, audio, 3D shape, CT reconstruction, super-resolution, NeRF).
Improvements are substantial, with up to 9 dB PSNR gains over state-of-the-art methods in some cases.
The work shifts focus from architectural design to optimization, showing that optimizer choice is a critical and underexplored aspect of INR training.
papers.limitation:
Muon is an extreme form of orthogonalization and may not represent an optimal solution, but rather a step towards a broader class of optimization strategies.
Periodic INRs such as SIREN and FINER did not converge for small model footprints in shape representation tasks, independent of optimization.
future_direction: Further exploration of optimization strategies that balance expressivity, smoothness, and generalization for implicit neural representations.
Developing a broader class of optimization methods beyond extreme orthogonalization.
papers.abstract: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) based on vanilla Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are widely believed to be incapable of representing high-frequency content. This has directed research efforts towards architectural interventions, such as coordinate embeddings or specialized activation functions, to represent high-frequency signals. In this paper, we challenge the notion that the low-frequency bias of vanilla MLPs is an intrinsic, architectural limitation to learn high-frequency content, but instead a symptom of stable rank degradation during training. We empirically demonstrate that regulating the network's rank during training substantially improves the fidelity of the learned signal, rendering even simple MLP architectures expressive. Extensive experiments show that using optimizers like Muon, with high-rank, near-orthogonal updates, consistently enhances INR architectures even beyond simple ReLU MLPs. These substantial improvements hold across a diverse range of domains, including natural and medical images, and novel view synthesis, with up to 9 dB PSNR improvements over the previous state-of-the-art. Our project page, which includes code and experimental results, is available at: (https://muon-inrs.github.io).

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Understanding the Countably Infinite: Neural Network Models of the Successor Function and its Acquisition
papers.research_question: How do children learn the successor function, what latent number representations make this possible, and what does it mean to understand the countably infinite?
papers.core_contribution: The place-value model shows a drop in representational similarity across tens boundaries, revealing that counting across a tens boundary can be understood as a vector operation in 2D space, and curriculum learning shows sharpening of smaller number representations during development.
papers.conclusion: This study is a first step in using neural networks to understand the successor function, and future work should explore recurrent architectures for modeling the counting process more generally.
papers.key_findings:
The count list model achieved perfect training accuracy but 0% test accuracy, indicating no generalization.
The place-value model showed 24% test accuracy and sensitivity to tens boundaries in representational similarity.
MDS analysis revealed systematic mapping of numbers to successors across tens boundaries in the place-value model.
Curriculum learning simulations showed incremental learning and sharpening of representations for smaller numbers.
The models did not learn the successor function well for the highest test range (81-99) in curriculum learning.
papers.limitation:
The count list model lacks sensitivity to tens boundaries, which is critical for place-value structure.
The place-value model has low test accuracy (24%) and does not generalize perfectly.
The models learn formally different ML tasks, making direct comparison difficult.
In curriculum learning, the highest test range (81-99) was not learned well even with additional training.
future_direction: Move beyond generating the successor of a number to modeling the counting process more generally.
Explore training recurrent neural network models to sequentially count, first to 100 and then arbitrarily high.
Use richer recurrent architectures to learn the recursive structure of natural numbers.
papers.abstract: As children enter elementary school, their understanding of the ordinal structure of numbers transitions from a memorized count list of the first 50-100 numbers to knowing the successor function and understanding the countably infinite. We investigate this developmental change in two neural network models that learn the successor function on the pairs (N, N+1) for N in (0, 98). The first uses a one-hot encoding of the input and output values and corresponds to children memorizing a count list, while the second model uses a place-value encoding and corresponds to children learning the language rules for naming numbers. The place-value model showed a predicted drop in representational similarity across tens boundaries. Counting across a tens boundary can be understood as a vector operation in 2D space, where the numbers with the same tens place are organized in a linearly separable manner, whereas those with the same ones place are grouped together. A curriculum learning simulation shows that, in the expanding numerical environment of the developing child, representations of smaller numbers continue to be sharpened even as larger numbers begin to be learned. These models set the stage for future work using recurrent architectures to move beyond learning the successor function to simulating the counting process more generally, and point towards a deeper understanding of what it means to understand the countably infinite.

papers.title: The Mechanistic Emergence of Symbol Grounding in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does symbol grounding emerge in language models, specifically what are the loci and mechanisms driving this emergence?
papers.core_contribution: Symbol grounding emerges in middle-layer computations via aggregate attention heads that retrieve environmental grounds to predict linguistic forms, generalizing across Transformers and state-space models but not LSTMs.
papers.conclusion: Symbol grounding can mechanistically emerge in autoregressive language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations.
Grounding is implemented through an aggregate mechanism where attention heads aggregate environmental ground to support prediction of linguistic forms.
This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models) but not in unidirectional LSTMs.
Grounding cannot be fully explained by co-occurrence statistics.
Causal interventions show that aggregate heads are critical for grounding.
papers.limitation: Full-scale VLMs present additional complications such as large numbers of visual tokens and redundant artifact tokens, making systematic identification and intervention at scale a nontrivial challenge.
future_direction: Investigate how grounding mechanisms interact with other emergent phenomena, such as in-context learning and reasoning.
Scale the analysis to larger models and more naturalistic settings.
papers.abstract: Symbol grounding (Harnad, 1990) describes how symbols such as words acquire their meanings by connecting to real-world sensorimotor experiences. Recent work has shown preliminary evidence that grounding may emerge in (vision-)language models trained at scale without using explicit grounding objectives. Yet, the specific loci of this emergence and the mechanisms that drive it remain largely unexplored. To address this problem, we introduce a controlled evaluation framework that systematically traces how symbol grounding arises within the internal computations through mechanistic and causal analysis. Our findings show that grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations and is implemented through the aggregate mechanism, where attention heads aggregate the environmental ground to support the prediction of linguistic forms. This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models), but not in unidirectional LSTMs. Our results provide behavioral and mechanistic evidence that symbol grounding can emerge in language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects: Discrepancy between Performance and Competence
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between performance and competence in LLMs' linguistic understanding? How do LLMs represent form and meaning across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurolinguistic method (minimal pair probing) to assess LLMs' linguistic competence, revealing a distinction between performance and competence, and showing LLMs have stronger form competence than meaning competence.
papers.conclusion: This study adopts both psycho- and neuro-linguistic approaches to evaluating LLMs, revealing a distinction between linguistic performance and competence, and highlights the limitations of LLMs' semantic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct.
Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence.
Instruction tuning improves performance but does not significantly change competence.
LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning.
LLMs encode form earlier than meaning.
papers.limitation:
Limited range of languages covered in experiments.
Poor German evaluation results potentially due to very long sentences in the DistilLingEval dataset.
Experiments conducted on small-scale LLMs due to computational resource constraints.
COMPS dataset for conceptual understanding is not sufficiently fine-grained, limited to only four types of conceptual relationships.
future_direction: Include experiments covering a wider range of languages.
Construct syntactic minimal pair datasets for German.
Explore larger models to validate and extend generalizability.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the linguistic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) regarding signifier (form) and signified (meaning) by distinguishing two LLM assessment paradigms: psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic. Traditional psycholinguistic evaluations often reflect statistical rules that may not accurately represent LLMs' true linguistic competence. We introduce a neurolinguistic approach, utilizing a novel method that combines minimal pair and diagnostic probing to analyze activation patterns across model layers. This method allows for a detailed examination of how LLMs represent form and meaning, and whether these representations are consistent across languages. We found: (1) Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct; (2) Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence; (3) Instruction tuning won't change much competence but improve performance; (4) LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning. Additionally, we introduce new conceptual minimal pair datasets for Chinese (COMPS-ZH) and German (COMPS-DE), complementing existing English datasets.

papers.title: Just-in-time and distributed task representations in language models
papers.research_question: When are transferrable task representations formed in language models during in-context learning, and how do they change over the context?
papers.core_contribution: Transferrable task representations in language models evolve non-monotonically and sporadically, activating only at key tokens, while a persistent representation of task identity is maintained throughout the context.
papers.conclusion: Language models form multiple types of task representations during in-context learning, with transferrable representations activating sporadically and task identity persisting, revealing a complex and nuanced dynamic of the model's internal state.
papers.key_findings:
Transferrable task representations (e.g., task vectors) accrue evidence from multiple in-context examples but form sporadically and non-monotonically.
Task identity representations are robustly decodable from residual activations across most tokens in the context, persisting throughout.
Transferrable task representations exhibit strong temporal locality, forming effectively only at specific tokens (e.g., the colon token before answer generation).
In longer- and mixed-generation tasks, transferrable task representations often decay over output units, showing semantic locality and limited task scope.
For complex tasks requiring state tracking or combining distinct subtasks, effective task representations are more distributed across tokens.
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot recontextualization remains challenging for tasks that require intermediate-state tracking or more complicated computation.
Overriding token activations at intermediate layers with task vectors may cause the model to lose task state information formed in earlier layers.
future_direction: Study the mechanistic bases for the strong temporal and scope locality observed in models' in-context transferrable task representations.
papers.abstract: Many of language models' impressive capabilities originate from their in-context learning: based on instructions or examples, they can infer and perform new tasks without weight updates. In this work, we investigate when representations for new tasks are formed in language models, and how these representations change over the course of context. We study two different task representations: those that are ''transferrable'' -- vector representations that can transfer task contexts to another model instance, even without the full prompt -- and simpler representations of high-level task categories. We show that transferrable task representations evolve in non-monotonic and sporadic ways, while task identity representations persist throughout the context. Specifically, transferrable task representations exhibit a two-fold locality. They successfully condense evidence when more examples are provided in the context. But this evidence accrual process exhibits strong temporal locality along the sequence dimension, coming online only at certain tokens -- despite task identity being reliably decodable throughout the context.
